{
  "lesson_key": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding",
  "title": "Hello Agentic Coding",
  "course": "TAC",
  "order": 1,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/hello-agentic-coding",
  "video": {
    "file": "tac-1-hello-agentic-coding/video/tac-1-hello-agentic-coding.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 1311,
    "duration_display": "21:51"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Stop Coding",
    "one_liner": "Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code — hand the typing to agents and move your engineering cycles up the stack.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks career engineers to retire the skill that defined them. Dan spent over a decade at startups and large companies typing code by hand — mastering languages, syntax, algorithms, data structures — and says he misses it too. The tactic demands you trust that language models running in agentic loops on supercomputers are now vastly superior coders, and that clinging to hand-typing means you have no chance of keeping up. Evolution forces us to leave skills behind to adopt new ones."
  },
  "mission": "Transform you into an engineer they can't replace — 'they' being your boss, the company, the industry, and AI itself. In a world where code is a commodity and your grandma or little brother can build an app with one prompt, you become irreplaceable the way engineers always have in technological revolutions: move up the stack. Become a commander of compute that builds systems that build systems, until your codebase runs itself.",
  "phase_model": {
    "phase1_ai_coding": "The generative-AI age's first phase: prompt-to-generate-code. Birth of vibe coders and the complete commoditization of code. You interact with the big three — context, model, prompt — to build faster than ever. Still foundational, no longer differentiating.",
    "phase2_agentic_coding": "Where real engineers strike back. A superset of AI coding: the big three plus tools — prompts that reliably execute long chains of tool calls inside an agentic coding tool. Engineers reallocate their cycles to planning, reviewing, and creating closed-loop structures, and turn their codebases into increasingly self-operating machines."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "agentic-engineer",
      "name": "The Agentic Engineer — a new role",
      "plain_english": "A software engineer whose job is not writing code but building systems that can take actions the way an engineer would: branch, write, run, test, commit, report. Dan bought agenticengineer.com in 2023 betting this role would emerge; lesson 1 declares it now exists.",
      "dan_words": "\"Predicting that a new role of software engineering would emerge, defined by the ability to build systems that can take actions as we can. It's become clear this new role now exists.\"",
      "misconception": "That 'agentic engineer' is a rebrand of 'prompt engineer.' It isn't: the role is defined by system-building (embedding agents across the SDLC), not by writing clever one-off prompts."
    },
    {
      "id": "phase-one-vs-phase-two",
      "name": "Phase 1 (AI coding) vs Phase 2 (agentic coding)",
      "plain_english": "Phase 1 = using AI to generate code faster (context, model, prompt). Phase 2 = using AI to perform engineering work end-to-end (add tools). The lesson's entire arc is the delta between these two phases, demonstrated with two prompts in one README.",
      "dan_words": "\"In the generative AI age, AI coding was phase one. Here we saw the birth of VibeCoders and the complete commoditization of code... Agentic coding marks phase two. This is where real engineers strike back.\"",
      "misconception": "That phase 2 replaces phase 1 knowledge. Agentic coding is a superset of AI coding — the big three are still there, always, even when you can't see them."
    },
    {
      "id": "stop-coding",
      "name": "Tactic #1: Stop Coding",
      "plain_english": "Stop typing code by hand. Not stop shipping code, not stop reading code — stop being the instrument that types it. Use the best tool for the job: agentic loops running powerful language models. Throughout all of TAC, not a single line of code is typed by hand.",
      "dan_words": "\"Let's end the debate right now. Your hands and your mind are no longer the best tool for the job of writing code, full stop.\"",
      "misconception": "Two opposite failure readings: (1) 'so we don't generate code anymore' — wrong, code is still a primary asset and you'll generate more than ever; (2) 'so I can stop understanding code' — wrong, code understanding is still critically important. What ends is hand-typing, and what replaces it is planning, reviewing, and closed-loop structures."
    },
    {
      "id": "commander-of-compute",
      "name": "Commander of Compute",
      "plain_english": "The identity shift of phase 2: your job is deciding where compute gets aimed and what systems it builds, not producing keystrokes. You don't just prompt to generate code — you direct compute to build systems that build systems.",
      "dan_words": "\"We move up the stack once again. We become a commander of compute... You take this compute and you use it to build systems that build systems.\"",
      "misconception": "That commanding compute means firing off more prompts manually. The command is structural — triggers, scripts, workflows that fire agents at the right time — not a human clicking faster."
    },
    {
      "id": "big-three",
      "name": "The Big Three (context, model, prompt)",
      "plain_english": "The three primitives of phase-1 AI coding: what the model can see (context), which model does the work (model), and what you ask for (prompt). Every AI coding interaction is governed by these whether you notice or not.",
      "dan_words": "\"With AI coding, you've been interacting with the big three: context, model, prompt. This is a principle of AI coding. It's always there even if you can't see it.\"",
      "misconception": "That the big three become obsolete in phase 2. They remain the foundation; phase 2 adds exactly one new dimension on top."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four",
      "name": "The Core Four (context, model, prompt, tools)",
      "plain_english": "Add tools to the big three and you get the core four — the primitives of agentic coding. The 'tools' element specifically means prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tool calls, not the mere existence of tool calling.",
      "dan_words": "\"The new element that transforms the big three of AI coding to Agentic Coding is prompts that can reliably execute long chains of tools. When you add tools, we upgrade the big three to the core four.\"",
      "misconception": "'Tool calling has been around for a while, this is not new.' Dan's rebuttal: you're 100% right — and it's not a question of new, it's a question of scale and performance. Reliable long-chain execution is what changed."
    },
    {
      "id": "agentic-prompt",
      "name": "The Agentic (Coding) Prompt",
      "plain_english": "A prompt that contains a sequence of tool calls — a workflow specification, not a text request. It reads like a runbook (RUN / CREATE / RUN / REPORT) and executes like one: branch, write files, run programs, commit, report. It is the unit of engineering work in TAC, and every later lesson scales it.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything we do in TAC is built upon this core idea you can see right in this readme with just 35 lines... A prompt contains a sequence of tool calls.\"",
      "misconception": "That it's 'just a prompt' — everyone knows prompts can call tools now. People don't invest the time to understand what this means at scale: fired repeatedly, with the right triggers and leverage, one prompt becomes an end-to-end developer workflow running minutes to hours without you."
    },
    {
      "id": "claude-code-form-factor",
      "name": "Claude Code's three essential elements",
      "plain_english": "Claude Code is the first agentic coding tool to properly combine: (1) a powerful language model that can reason when needed, (2) the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and (3) the right agent architecture. That combination — being copied by every other tool — unlocks the core four, which unlocks the agentic prompt.",
      "dan_words": "\"Claude Code is the first Agentic Coding tool to properly combine three essential elements: a powerful language model that can reason when needed, the ability to consistently call long chains of tools, and the right agent architecture... Reliable Agentic Coding at scale was not possible before Claude Code.\"",
      "misconception": "That the lesson is Claude Code marketing and expires with the tool. Dan pre-handles this: your UI may differ, your models will be newer — great. The tactics are transferable to any tool with the right capabilities; don't get stuck on any one tool."
    },
    {
      "id": "programmable-agentic-coding",
      "name": "Programmable agentic coding (claude -p)",
      "plain_english": "Because Claude Code runs in the terminal, any language with terminal access can invoke it as a function: read a prompt file, pass it to `claude -p`, capture the output. 309	    "Match the model to the task (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus) — the model is rarely the bottleneck now; your ability to wield agents is.",

{
  "lesson_key": "ah-3-building-domain-specific-agents",
  "title": "Building Domain-Specific Agents",
  "course": "AH",
  "order": 11,
  "lesson_url": "https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/building-domain-specific-agents",
  "video": {
    "file": "ah-3-building-domain-specific-agents/video/ah-3-building-domain-specific-agents.mp4",
    "duration_seconds": 4030,
    "duration_display": "1:07:10",
    "resolution": "1920x1080"
  },
  "tactic": {
    "name": "Build Custom Agents",
    "one_liner": "When out-of-the-box agents stop fitting your domain, stop renting someone else's agent and build your own: take programmatic control of the core four (context, model, prompt, tools) in code so your compute works for your problems, your edge cases, your codebase — not everyone's.",
    "why_uncomfortable": "It asks engineers who just learned to love Claude Code to admit the tool they love is built for everyone's codebase, not theirs — and that the gap costs hundreds of hours and millions of tokens as their codebase grows. Worse, it demands you overwrite the system prompt of the best agent on the market ('this is not Claude Code anymore'), throwing away all the work the Claude Code team baked in, and trust that YOUR three-line prompt plus a few tools will serve your domain better than their generalist. Dan repeatedly de-escalates the discomfort: you usually should NOT build a custom agent; extend before you overwrite; never try to out-engineer Claude Code at general engineering. The tactic is a scalpel for the last-mile domain problems, not a hammer for everything."
  },
  "mission": "Give you programmatic mastery over agents so you can deploy effective compute anywhere across your stack, products, and engineering lifecycle. By the end you can look at any repeat, domain-specific, or out-of-loop problem and know whether to reach for the out-of-the-box agent, an extended agent, or a complete custom agent — and if custom, build it from a 150-line script up to a multi-agent web application by controlling the core four in code. The deeper mission of the Agentic Horizon: agentic coding is no longer about what YOU can do, it's about what you can teach your agents to do.",
  "progression_model": {
    "the_path": "Agentic engineering leads every engineer down one single path: better agents -> more agents -> custom agents. First you learn to prompt- and context-engineer a single agent well (better). Then you scale compute by delegating to subagents and new primary agents (more). Then, only when you hit domain-specific walls out-of-the-box tools can't clear, you go to the bare metal: custom agents.",
    "better_agents": "Prompt engineering and context engineering a single agent until it performs. This is the foundation the whole Agentic Horizon builds on (RD framework, agentic prompt formats).",
    "more_agents": "Scale your compute to scale your impact by delegating work to subagents and additional primary agents (multi-agent orchestration).",
    "custom_agents": "The bare metal. Build agents whose context, model, prompt, and tools you control in code — tailored to your domain-specific problems, protected from calling the wrong tools at the wrong time, and deployable programmatically anywhere (scripts, streams, terminals, UIs, backends)."
  },
  "core_concepts": [
    {
      "id": "system-prompt-is-everything",
      "name": "The system prompt is the law of the agent",
      "plain_english": "The system prompt is the single most important element of a custom agent, with zero exceptions. It is injected before every user prompt, so it multiplies (governs) every single run the agent will ever do. The Pong agent proves it: two tiny changes to a Claude Agent SDK config (model + a 3-line system prompt) turn the world's best coding agent into a thing that replies 'pong' to literally anything. Overwrite the system prompt and you have a new product — same model, entirely different agent.",
      "dan_words": "\"The system prompt is the most important element of your custom agents, with zero exceptions... The system prompt affects every single user prompt the agent runs, every single one. So all of your work is multiplied by your system prompt.\"",
      "misconception": "That a custom agent needs lots of code. Pong is ~150 lines and most of it is logging; the behavior-defining change is a 3-line markdown file. The leverage is in the prompt, not the plumbing."
    },
    {
      "id": "not-claude-code-anymore",
      "name": "Overwrite the system prompt and it's not Claude Code anymore",
      "plain_english": "The moment you fully replace the system prompt, you have discarded everything the Claude Code team engineered into their agent and created a brand-new product. It might use the same model, but it is not Claude Code. This is powerful and dangerous: you gain total control and lose all the built-in generalist competence. Alternative: you can APPEND to the preset Claude Code system prompt instead of overwriting it — an extension, not a replacement.",
      "dan_words": "\"This is not the Claude Code product anymore. As soon as you touch the system prompt and once you start dialing into the tools, you change the product, you change the agent... it is important to mention you can append system prompt.\"",
      "misconception": "That custom always means overwrite. Overwrite is one end of a spectrum; append (extend) is the other, and most engineering work only needs a light extension."
    },
    {
      "id": "core-four-in-code",
      "name": "Custom agents let you control the core four in code",
      "plain_english": "The core four — context, model, prompt, tools — are the primitives of every agent (from the 12 leverage points of agentic coding). Out-of-the-box you accept the defaults. A custom agent, via the Claude Agent SDK's options object, lets you set each one explicitly and consistently: which model, what system/user prompts, which tools are allowed or disallowed, what MCP servers and configs load. 'This is quite literally in code, so our agent will always perform this way.' Isolate the core four in any agent config and you understand and can scale your compute.",
      "dan_words": "\"Whenever you see Claude Code options, isolate the core four. How will the core four be managed given this setup?... Custom agents let you control all of these very quickly and consistently.\"",
      "misconception": "That the core four is abstract theory. In the SDK it is a concrete options object — every field maps to one of the four, and the user prompt arrives via client.query()."
    },
    {
      "id": "everything-ends-up-in-context",
      "name": "Everything you give an agent ends up in its context window",
      "plain_english": "Tools, MCP servers, system prompt, user prompt — all of it consumes space in the agent's 'mind.' The Echo agent proves that even after you add one custom tool, the ~15 baked-in Claude Code tools are STILL loaded (15 extra options the model must consider and pay tokens for). The Calc agent shows the fix: an explicit disallowed_tools list removes those tools entirely — they are no longer even an option, they don't reach the context window. Adopt your agent's perspective; run /context; control the knob.",
      "dan_words": "\"Everything that's going into your agent winds up in the context window at some point. We have 15 extra tools, 15 extra options that our agent has to choose from... It consumes space in your agent's mind.\"",
      "misconception": "That setting allowed_tools is enough to keep the context lean. allowed_tools gates what CAN be called; the built-in tool definitions still load unless you disallow them. Disallowing removes them from context entirely."
    },
    {
      "id": "model-selection",
      "name": "Match the model to the task",
      "plain_english": "A custom agent explicitly declares its model, so you right-size intelligence to the job. Echo is a trivial transform, so Dan downgrades it to Claude Haiku — cheaper, less intelligent, much faster. Calc and most others use Sonnet (balanced); the SDLC agent offers Opus for the smart planning/review steps. 'It's not the models that are the limitation anymore. It's you and I — our ability to wield better, more, and custom agents.'",
      "dan_words": "\"We're running Claude Haiku. We have downgraded our model to a cheaper, less intelligent, but much faster model... This is a simple agent. It doesn't need powerful intelligence.\"",
      "misconception": "That a stronger model is always better. For simple, high-volume, or latency-sensitive tools, a smaller model is the correct engineering choice — and cheaper at scale."
    },
    {
      "id": "custom-tools-and-mcp",
      "name": "Custom tools and in-memory MCP servers",
      "plain_english": "You give an agent new capabilities with the @tool decorator (name, description, typed params) and mount them via create_sdk_mcp_server — an entire MCP server built in memory for your agent. The tool's DESCRIPTION tells the agent when/how to use it; inside the tool you are back in deterministic code — do anything, then return the proper format. Custom agents can also tap the existing MCP ecosystem (the QA agent loads the Firecrawl MCP server via an .mcp.json config, ~6k tokens) — you don't have to reinvent tools that already exist.",
      "dan_words": "\"This builds an entire MCP server in memory for our agent... The description of your tool tells your agent how to use it, in addition to the actual parameters. 1	# AH-3 Lab Spec — Building Domain-Specific Agents
2	
3	**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only — `agentic-horizon/building-specialized-agents` (resolve the lesson symlink `.../ah-3-building-domain-specific-agents/codebase`, or clone the lesson repo from the loot box). No external repos.
4	**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you never hand-edit an agent to "fix" it — you either configure it via `ClaudeAgentOptions` or, in the stretch drills, change it *through* Claude Code. You're learning to command custom agents, not to babysit them.
5	**Time box:** 90–150 minutes (it's an advanced, 8-agent lesson). **Token/cost note:** the CLI agents (1–5) are cheap; the UI agents (6–8) and the Social Hype firehose can burn real tokens — budget for it, and stop streams when done.
6	**Reading skill graded above all:** for every agent you touch, you must be able to point at its `ClaudeAgentOptions` and name how each of the **core four** (context, model, prompt, tools) is set.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 0 · Setup (15 min)
11	
12	1. Enter the codebase: `cd agentic-horizon/building-specialized-agents` (or your clone). Skim `README.md` — it lists all eight agents with run commands.
13	2. Verify the toolbelt: `uv --version`, `claude --version`, `node --version` (+ `bun --version` for the Vue frontends).
14	3. `cp .env.sample .env` and set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (or use a Claude plan). Optional: `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` (QA agent), `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` (Social Hype TTS). macOS is assumed for Social Hype `osascript` alerts.
15	4. **SDK sanity check:** open any agent's `pyproject.toml`. Confirm the dependency reads **`claude-agent-sdk`** and the `.py` imports **`ClaudeAgentOptions`** — *not* `ClaudeCodeOptions`. (This is the recorded-vs-current rename; the video/frames say the old name.)
16	
17	**Checkpoint 0:** you can state the package name (`claude-agent-sdk`) and the options class (`ClaudeAgentOptions`) without looking, and you know why the video says "Claude Code SDK."
18	
19	---
20	
21	## 1 · The reading drill — find the core four (20 min)
22	
23	Open, in order, `custom_1_pong_agent/pong_agent.py`, `custom_2_echo_agent/echo_agent.py`, `custom_3_calc_agent/calc_agent.py`. For **each**, locate the `ClaudeAgentOptions(...)` block and fill this table (write it down):
24	
25	| Agent | context (allowed/disallowed/MCP) | model | prompt (overwrite/append; any `{VAR}`) | tools (custom? which?) |
26	|-------|----------------------------------|-------|----------------------------------------|------------------------|
27	
28	**Checkpoint 1:** your table shows Pong (no tools, Sonnet, overwrite), Echo (1 custom `echo` tool via in-memory MCP, **Haiku**, overwrite), Calc (2 custom tools, **explicit `disallowed_tools`**, Sonnet, `resume=`). You can explain why Pong uses `query()` while Echo/Calc use `ClaudeSDKClient`.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## 2 · Run the ladder & prove the system prompt is the law (20 min)
33	
34	1. `uv run python apps/custom_1_pong_agent/pong_agent.py --prompt "summarize this codebase"` → it replies **pong**. Open `prompts/PONG_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md` and confirm the 3-line prompt is the *only* thing defining that behavior.
35	2. `uv run python apps/custom_2_echo_agent/echo_agent.py "echo 'custom agents' in reverse uppercase repeat 2"` → watch the **Tool Called** block, then the transformed result.
36	3. `uv run python apps/custom_3_calc_agent/calc_agent.py` → ask "convert 55 fahrenheit to celsius", then "what was my last calculation?" (proves `resume=` memory). Type `quit`.
37	
38	**Checkpoint 2:** you can state, in one sentence, why changing *only* the system prompt turns Claude Code into a "pong machine" — and that overwriting it means "this is not Claude Code anymore."
39	
40	---
41	
42	## 3 · The context experiment — allowed vs disallowed (15 min) ⭐
43	
44	This is the money drill.
45	1. In the Echo agent, ask it: `uv run python apps/custom_2_echo_agent/echo_agent.py "list your available tools"`. Count them. You added **one** tool — how many does it list?
46	2. Now run the Calc agent and ask "list all your tools, names only." Count again.
47	3. Explain the difference by reading the two options blocks: Echo sets `allowed_tools` but **not** `disallowed_tools`; Calc sets a full `disallowed_tools` list.
48	
49	**Checkpoint 3 (write it down):** *`allowed_tools` gates what can be **called**; the ~15 built-in tools are still **loaded into context** unless you **disallow** them.* State which agent proves each half of that sentence.
50	
51	---
52	
53	## 4 · Governance — hooks that say no (20 min)
54	
55	1. Launch the QA agent: `uv run python apps/custom_5_qa_agent/qa_agent.py`.
56	2. Ask it: `read the .env.sample file`. Watch the **🔒 SECURITY HOOK** panel deny the read and explain why.
57	3. Open `qa_agent.py` → `block_env_files`. Trace the return value: `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision == "deny"`. Note the second hook, `log_tool_usage` (audit).
58	4. Run the shipped hook test: `uv run python apps/custom_5_qa_agent/test_inline_hooks.py`. Confirm it exercises the `.env` block.
59	5. Ask QA a real question ("how does the QA agent handle security hooks? think hard") and watch the **Thinking** block + any parallel `Task` subagents.
60	
61	**Checkpoint 4:** you can explain what the hook returns to block a call, and confirm (from Dan's claim + the code) that hooks also cover **subagents**. Bonus: note that the agent gracefully fell back to WebSearch/WebFetch if you didn't rename `.mcp.json.firecrawl_6k.sample`.
62	
63	---
64	
65	## 5 · Agents in UIs (25 min)
66	
67	Pick **at least two** of the three UI agents (do Ultra Stream — it's the flagship).
68	
69	**A. Tri-Copy-Writer (one prompt → N variations).**
70	- Backend: `cd apps/custom_6_tri_copy_writer/backend && uv sync && uv run python main.py -v 6`
71	- Frontend: `cd ../frontend && npm install && npm run dev` → open http://127.0.0.1:5173
72	- Prompt "write a blog post title for a productivity app." Confirm **6** variations. In `backend/main.py`, find `disallowed_tools` (ALL tools off) and the `CopyResponse` **Pydantic** model; in the system prompt, find `{NUMBER_OF_VERSIONS}`.
73	
74	**B. Micro SDLC (multi-agent hand-off).**
75	- Start backend + frontend per README; open the kanban board.
76	- Create a ticket, e.g. "update the HTML title and header to 'Plan, Build, Review, Ship Agents'"; drag it to **Plan** and watch it flow Plan → Build → Review → Shipped over the WebSocket log.
77	- In `backend/modules/agent_orchestrator.py`, confirm: **planner** = preset+`append`+write-hook to `specs/`; **builder** = *pure* `claude_code` preset (no append); **reviewer** = preset+`append`+write-hook to `reviews/`.
78	
79	**C. Ultra Stream (dual producer/consumer agents).**
80	- `cd apps/custom_8_ultra_stream_agent && uv sync && uv run python backend/main.py --reset` (+ frontend). Watch the **Stream** agent summarize the log feed with severities and raise a HIGH alert.
81	- Ask the **Inspector** agent "list issues 1–3, log summary only" and "find logs for user <id>, summary only."
82	- In `backend/main.py`, read `read_stream_file` (note the `sed` subprocess + `raw_log_cache`) and `clear_context`.
83	
84	**Checkpoint 5:** for each UI agent you ran, name the SDK surface (custom tools? disallowed all? preset+append? `resume`?) and state what problem the UI solves that a script couldn't.
85	
86	---
87	
88	## 6 · Judgment drill — when custom, when not (10 min)
89	
90	Write two short lists from your own work:
91	1. Three tasks that are **custom-agent-shaped** (programmatic / repeat / domain-specific / permission-gated / out-of-loop).
92	2. Three tasks that should stay on the **out-of-the-box or extended** agent (in-loop / generic / prototyping / one-off).
93	Then pick the **one** custom-agent-shaped task you'd build first, and name which of the eight lesson agents is its closest template.
94	
95	**Checkpoint 6:** your first pick is genuinely out-of-loop or domain-specific — not something Claude Code already does well in-loop.
96	
97	---
98	
99	## Stretch (optional, +30–45 min) — change agents *through* Claude Code
100	
101	Type zero lines of application code by hand for these.
102	1. **Model swap:** have Claude Code change the Echo agent's model line to a current Haiku-class ID and rerun; confirm it still echoes.
103	2. **New tool:** have Claude Code add a third tool to the Calc agent (e.g. `custom_percentage`), register it in `create_sdk_mcp_server`, add it to `allowed_tools`, and prove it fires.
104	3. **Tighten governance:** extend the QA hook to also **deny** reads of `*.pem`/`*.key` (today they only warn). Test with a fake key file, then delete it.
105	4. **Extend, don't overwrite:** in the Micro SDLC agent, add one line to the planner's *appended* instructions and confirm via the run log that the builder (pure preset) is unaffected.
106	5. **Harden a tool:** replace Calc's `eval()` with an `ast`-based evaluator; verify the same conversions still work and that `import os` in an expression is rejected.
107	
108	**Stretch checkpoint:** every change went through the agent or through `ClaudeAgentOptions` — you never hand-patched behavior the config should own.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## Pass criteria (all must hold)
113	
114	- [ ] You can point at any agent's `ClaudeAgentOptions` and name how each of the **core four** is set.
115	- [ ] You state the SDK's real name (`claude-agent-sdk` / `ClaudeAgentOptions`) and why the video says "Claude Code SDK."
116	- [ ] You demonstrated the **allowed vs disallowed** context lesson from the Echo→Calc contrast (Checkpoint 3), in your own words.
117	- [ ] You triggered the QA `.env` **deny** hook and can explain the returned `permissionDecision` (Checkpoint 4).
118	- [ ] You ran ≥2 UI agents including **Ultra Stream**, and can explain how its Stream agent processes a file bigger than its context window.
119	- [ ] You can articulate the **extend vs overwrite** distinction using the SDLC builder (pure preset) as evidence.
120	- [ ] You produced your custom-vs-generalist lists and named your first build + its template agent.
121	
122	---
123	
124	## Instructor / self-grader notes
125	
126	- The **highest-value single drill is #3** (context experiment). If a student only "gets" one thing, it must be that `disallowed_tools` — not `allowed_tools` — is what keeps the context window lean.
127	- Common stumble: students conflate a **system-prompt** static variable (`{NOTIFICATION_CRITERIA}`, `{NUMBER_OF_VERSIONS}`, locked at boot) with a **user-prompt** dynamic variable (`$1`/`$ARGUMENTS`). Probe for this in Part 5A.
128	- If Firecrawl isn't configured, the QA agent still passes (it falls back to WebSearch). Don't fail a student for the `.mcp.json.firecrawl_6k.sample` rename gotcha — flag it as the intended setup lesson.
129	- Watch for the anti-pattern the whole lesson warns against: a student building a custom agent for in-loop generic work. Redirect them to "just use Claude Code" — that judgment IS the lesson's finale.
130	- Stop the Social Hype firehose and the UI backends when done; they hold WebSocket connections and can quietly accrue tokens.
131

4. **SDK sanity check:** open any agent's `pyproject.toml`. Confirm the dependency reads **`claude-agent-sdk`** and the `.py` imports **`ClaudeAgentOptions`** — *not* `ClaudeCodeOptions`. (This is the recorded-vs-current rename; the video/frames say the old name.)

**Checkpoint 0:** you can state the package name (`claude-agent-sdk`) and the options class (`ClaudeAgentOptions`) without looking, and you know why the video says "Claude Code SDK."

---

## 1 · The reading drill — find the core four (20 min)

Open, in order, `custom_1_pong_agent/pong_agent.py`, `custom_2_echo_agent/echo_agent.py`, `custom_3_calc_agent/calc_agent.py`. For **each**, locate the `ClaudeAgentOptions(...)` block and fill this table (write it down):

| Agent | context (allowed/disallowed/MCP) | model | prompt (overwrite/append; any `{VAR}`) | tools (custom? which?) |
|-------|----------------------------------|-------|----------------------------------------|------------------------|

**Checkpoint 1:** your table shows Pong (no tools, Sonnet, overwrite), Echo (1 custom `echo` tool via in-memory MCP, **Haiku**, overwrite), Calc (2 custom tools, **explicit `disallowed_tools`**, Sonnet, `resume=`). You can explain why Pong uses `query()` while Echo/Calc use `ClaudeSDKClient`.

---

## 2 · Run the ladder & prove the system prompt is the law (20 min)

1. `uv run python apps/custom_1_pong_agent/pong_agent.py --prompt "summarize this codebase"` → it replies **pong**. Open `prompts/PONG_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT.md` and confirm the 3-line prompt is the *only* thing defining that behavior.
2. `uv run python apps/custom_2_echo_agent/echo_agent.py "echo 'custom agents' in reverse uppercase repeat 2"` → watch the **Tool Called** block, then the transformed result.
3. `uv run python apps/custom_3_calc_agent/calc_agent.py` → ask "convert 55 fahrenheit to celsius", then "what was my last calculation?" (proves `resume=` memory). Type `quit`.

**Checkpoint 2:** you can state, in one sentence, why changing *only* the system prompt turns Claude Code into a "pong machine" — and that overwriting it means "this is not Claude Code anymore."

---

## 3 · The context experiment — allowed vs disallowed (15 min) ⭐

This is the money drill.
1. In the Echo agent, ask it: `uv run python apps/custom_2_echo_agent/echo_agent.py "list your available tools"`. Count them. You added **one** tool — how many does it list?
2. Now run the Calc agent and ask "list all your tools, names only." Count again.
3. Explain the difference by reading the two options blocks: Echo sets `allowed_tools` but **not** `disallowed_tools`; Calc sets a full `disallowed_tools` list.

**Checkpoint 3 (write it down):** *`allowed_tools` gates what can be **called**; the ~15 built-in tools are still **loaded into context** unless you **disallow** them.* State which agent proves each half of that sentence.

---

## 4 · Governance — hooks that say no (20 min)

1. Launch the QA agent: `uv run python apps/custom_5_qa_agent/qa_agent.py`.
2. Ask it: `read the .env.sample file`. Watch the **🔒 SECURITY HOOK** panel deny the read and explain why.
3. Open `qa_agent.py` → `block_env_files`. Trace the return value: `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision == "deny"`. Note the second hook, `log_tool_usage` (audit).
4. Run the shipped hook test: `uv run python apps/custom_5_qa_agent/test_inline_hooks.py`. Confirm it exercises the `.env` block.
5. Ask QA a real question ("how does the QA agent handle security hooks? think hard") and watch the **Thinking** block + any parallel `Task` subagents.

**Checkpoint 4:** you can explain what the hook returns to block a call, and confirm (from Dan's claim + the code) that hooks also cover **subagents**. Bonus: note that the agent gracefully fell back to WebSearch/WebFetch if you didn't rename `.mcp.json.firecrawl_6k.sample`.

---

## 5 · Agents in UIs (25 min)

Pick **at least two** of the three UI agents (do Ultra Stream — it's the flagship).

**A. Tri-Copy-Writer (one prompt → N variations).**
- Backend: `cd apps/custom_6_tri_copy_writer/backend && uv sync && uv run python main.py -v 6`
- Frontend: `cd ../frontend && npm install && npm run dev` → open http://127.0.0.1:5173
- Prompt "write a blog post title for a productivity app." Confirm **6** variations. In `backend/main.py`, find `disallowed_tools` (ALL tools off) and the `CopyResponse` **Pydantic** model; in the system prompt, find `{NUMBER_OF_VERSIONS}`.

**B. Micro SDLC (multi-agent hand-off).**
- Start backend + frontend per README; open the kanban board.
- Create a ticket, e.g. "update the HTML title and header to 'Plan, Build, Review, Ship Agents'"; drag it to **Plan** and watch it flow Plan → Build → Review → Shipped over the WebSocket log.
- In `backend/modules/agent_orchestrator.py`, confirm: **planner** = preset+`append`+write-hook to `specs/`; **builder** = *pure* `claude_code` preset (no append); **reviewer** = preset+`append`+write-hook to `reviews/`.

**C. Ultra Stream (dual producer/consumer agents).**
- `cd apps/custom_8_ultra_stream_agent && uv sync && uv run python backend/main.py --reset` (+ frontend). Watch the **Stream** agent summarize the log feed with severities and raise a HIGH alert.
- Ask the **Inspector** agent "list issues 1–3, log summary only" and "find logs for user <id>, summary only."
- In `backend/main.py`, read `read_stream_file` (note the `sed` subprocess + `raw_log_cache`) and `clear_context`.

**Checkpoint 5:** for each UI agent you ran, name the SDK surface (custom tools? disallowed all? preset+append? `resume`?) and state what problem the UI solves that a script couldn't.

---

## 6 · Judgment drill — when custom, when not (10 min)

Write two short lists from your own work:
1. Three tasks that are **custom-agent-shaped** (programmatic / repeat / domain-specific / permission-gated / out-of-loop).
2. Three tasks that should stay on the **out-of-the-box or extended** agent (in-loop / generic / prototyping / one-off).
Then pick the **one** custom-agent-shaped task you'd build first, and name which of the eight lesson agents is its closest template.

**Checkpoint 6:** your first pick is genuinely out-of-loop or domain-specific — not something Claude Code already does well in-loop.

---

## Stretch (optional, +30–45 min) — change agents *through* Claude Code

Type zero lines of application code by hand for these.
1. **Model swap:** have Claude Code change the Echo agent's model line to a current Haiku-class ID and rerun; confirm it still echoes.
2. **New tool:** have Claude Code add a third tool to the Calc agent (e.g. `custom_percentage`), register it in `create_sdk_mcp_server`, add it to `allowed_tools`, and prove it fires.
3. **Tighten governance:** extend the QA hook to also **deny** reads of `*.pem`/`*.key` (today they only warn). Test with a fake key file, then delete it.
4. **Extend, don't overwrite:** in the Micro SDLC agent, add one line to the planner's *appended* instructions and confirm via the run log that the builder (pure preset) is unaffected.
5. **Harden a tool:** replace Calc's `eval()` with an `ast`-based evaluator; verify the same conversions still work and that `import os` in an expression is rejected.

**Stretch checkpoint:** every change went through the agent or through `ClaudeAgentOptions` — you never hand-patched behavior the config should own.

---

## Pass criteria (all must hold)

- [ ] You can point at any agent's `ClaudeAgentOptions` and name how each of the **core four** is set.
- [ ] You state the SDK's real name (`claude-agent-sdk` / `ClaudeAgentOptions`) and why the video says "Claude Code SDK."
- [ ] You demonstrated the **allowed vs disallowed** context lesson from the Echo→Calc contrast (Checkpoint 3), in your own words.
- [ ] You triggered the QA `.env` **deny** hook and can explain the returned `permissionDecision` (Checkpoint 4).
- [ ] You ran ≥2 UI agents including **Ultra Stream**, and can explain how its Stream agent processes a file bigger than its context window.
- [ ] You can articulate the **extend vs overwrite** distinction using the SDLC builder (pure preset) as evidence.
- [ ] You produced your custom-vs-generalist lists and named your first build + its template agent.

---

## Instructor / self-grader notes

- The **highest-value single drill is #3** (context experiment). If a student only "gets" one thing, it must be that `disallowed_tools` — not `allowed_tools` — is what keeps the context window lean.
- Common stumble: students conflate a **system-prompt** static variable (`{NOTIFICATION_CRITERIA}`, `{NUMBER_OF_VERSIONS}`, locked at boot) with a **user-prompt** dynamic variable (`$1`/`$ARGUMENTS`). Probe for this in Part 5A.
- If Firecrawl isn't configured, the QA agent still passes (it falls back to WebSearch). Don't fail a student for the `.mcp.json.firecrawl_6k.sample` rename gotcha — flag it as the intended setup lesson.
- Watch for the anti-pattern the whole lesson warns against: a student building a custom agent for in-loop generic work. Redirect them to "just use Claude Code" — that judgment IS the lesson's finale.
- Stop the Social Hype firehose and the UI backends when done; they hold WebSocket connections and can quietly accrue tokens.

# Multi-Agent Orchestration: One Agent To Rule Them All
**Lesson #12 (Advanced)**  ·  https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding/course/multi-agent-orchestration-the-o-agent

_Scale your agentic engineering with the one agent to rule them all: The Orchestrator Agent. Command fleets of specialized agents through a single interface with CRUD operations and real-time observability. Get ahead of the next paradigm in Agentic Coding._

## Loot Box — 11 notes

### 🔥 The Agent Evolution Path
Base agents → Better agents → More agents → Custom agents → Orchestrated agents. Each step scales your compute to scale your impact.

### 🔥 Orchestrate to Scale
Command your fleet of agents using the single interface pattern. The rate at which you create and command agents becomes your engineering output constraint.

### 🔥 The Single Interface Pattern
Talk to one orchestrator agent that creates, commands, and deletes specialized agents. One interface to rule them all.

### 🔥 The Three Pillars of Multi-Agent Orchestration
Orchestrator Agent (unified interface), CRUD for agents at scale, and Observability (real-time monitoring of performance, costs, and results).

### 🔥 Observability Is Key
If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. If you can't measure it, you can't scale it. Multi-agent observability is essential for success.

### 🔥 Managing The Core Four At Scale
Track context windows, models, prompts, and tools for every agent you spin up. Adopt your agent's perspective multiplied across your fleet.

### ⚔️ TAC Lesson 12 - Multi-Agent Orchestration Repository
git clone https://github.com/disler/multi-agent-orchestration.git

### ⚡ Claude Code Agent SDK Documentation
Official Python SDK documentation for building custom agents programmatically. The extensibility of Claude Code makes multi-agent orchestration possible.

### 🔥 Stay Out The Loop With Multi-Agent Systems
Multi-agent orchestration is an out-loop PITER system: Prompt input, Trigger (HTTP), Environment, and Review (observability). Compound your engineering leverage.

### 🔥 One Agent, One Prompt, One Purpose
Each specialized agent serves one purpose with a focused context window, produces concrete results, then gets deleted. Keep agents lean and focused.

### 🔥 R&D Framework For Multi-Agent Context
Reduce unnecessary context in your primary orchestrator, Delegate work to specialized sub-agents with focused context windows. Context mastery at scale. 1	# AH-3 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner
2	
3	Ordering rule: how much of custom-agent competence collapses if this nugget is missing. **Tier 1** is non-negotiable; **Tier 2** is the working machinery of the Claude Agent SDK; **Tier 3** is judgment — when to reach for a custom agent at all.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else
8	
9	**1. The path is fixed: better → more → custom agents.**
10	You don't decide to build custom agents; you *arrive* at them by pushing compute to its limits on a domain problem the out-of-the-box tools can't clear. Master one agent, then scale to many, then — only when the mismatch bites — go to the bare metal.
11	*Say it Dan's way:* "Agentic engineering leads every engineer down one single path. Better agents, more agents, and then custom agents."
12	
13	**2. The system prompt is the law of the agent — with zero exceptions.**
14	It runs before *every* user prompt, so all the agent's work is multiplied by it. Pong proves it: a 3-line system prompt turns the best coding agent on earth into a thing that says "pong" to anything. Change the system prompt and *"this is not Claude Code anymore."*
15	*Why weak learners lose it:* they think "custom agent" means lots of code. Pong is ~150 lines and most of it is logging.
16	
17	**3. A custom agent is just the core four set in code.**
18	Context, model, prompt, tools — declared explicitly in `ClaudeAgentOptions` so the agent behaves the same way every run. When you open any agent, find the options block and ask: *how is each of the core four being managed here?* That single habit lets you read any agent.
19	
20	**4. Everything you give an agent ends up in its context window — and costs tokens.**
21	Tools, MCP configs, system prompt, user prompt: all of it. Echo's gut-punch: add ONE custom tool and the ~15 built-in Claude Code tools are *still* loaded. `allowed_tools` gates what can be **called**; only `disallowed_tools` removes the definitions from **context**.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## Tier 2 — The working machinery (Claude Agent SDK)
26	
27	**5. `query()` is one-off; `ClaudeSDKClient` is a conversation — and the only path to custom tools.**
28	If your agent needs a custom tool or memory across turns, you need the client. Keep memory alive by capturing `ResultMessage.session_id` and passing it back as `resume=` on the next call.
29	
30	**6. A tool is deterministic code with a great description.**
31	`@tool("name","description",{param:type})` + `create_sdk_mcp_server(...)` = an MCP server built in memory. The **description** tells the agent *when* to call it; inside you do anything and return `{"content":[...]}`. On failure, return the error so the agent can **pivot** (the "stdout + tools" leverage point). Custom agents can also load *existing* MCP servers (QA → Firecrawl).
32	
33	**7. Manage the responses, or you're flying blind.**
34	The loop is always **options → agent → query → manage responses**. Parse `TextBlock` (answer), `ThinkingBlock` (reasoning), `ToolUseBlock` (a call), `ToolResultBlock` (a return), and `ResultMessage` (session/cost). Log everything — *"if you don't adopt your agent's perspective, it will be hard to improve them."*
35	
36	**8. Match the model to the task.**
37	Echo drops to **Haiku** (cheap, fast, less smart — perfect for a trivial transform); most agents use **Sonnet**; the SDLC agent offers **Opus** for heavy planning. *"It's not the models that are the bottleneck anymore. It's you and I."*
38	
39	**9. Static system-prompt variable ≠ dynamic user variable.**
40	`{NOTIFICATION_CRITERIA}` / `{NUMBER_OF_VERSIONS}` are set once at boot and **frozen** — right for a single-purpose agent. A true dynamic variable (`$1` / `$ARGUMENTS`) changes every user prompt. Don't confuse them.
41

43	`PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse` hooks can **deny** a tool call (QA blocks reading `.env`; the SDLC planner can write only to `specs/`). Return `permissionDecision: "deny"`. Hooks cover **subagents** too — the security boundary holds when the agent spawns `Task` agents.
44	
45	**11. Extend before you overwrite.**

47	
48	**12. Domain tools beat insurmountable problems cheaply.**
49	Ultra Stream's Stream agent reads a log file *bigger than its context window* by pulling 3–5 lines at a time (`sed` subprocess), summarizing one log per call, and calling `clear_context` to reset itself — infinite, token-efficient. *"You cannot do this without serious prompt engineering with an out-of-the-box agent."*
50	
51	**13. Agents deploy in every form factor — and can feed each other.**
52	Script → REPL → stream handler → backend method → full UI. And one agent's output can be another's input: Ultra Stream's Stream agent **produces** summaries the Inspector agent **consumes**.
53	
54	---
55

57	
58	**14. Build custom only when you need to.**
59	Build custom for: programmatic agents · repeat workflows · domain-specific wins · cost-down/performance-up · permission checks · staying **out of the loop**. Otherwise use out-of-the-box or lightly extended agents.
60	
61	**15. Do NOT try to out-build Claude Code.**
62	For in-loop, generic, exploratory, or one-off work, just use Claude Code. And never try to reproduce it as a general engineering agent — *"they own agentic coding… this space is totally oversaturated."* Custom agents are a scalpel for the last mile, not a replacement for the generalist.
63	
64	**16. Consistent codebase architecture is a leverage point.**
65	Every agent shares the same shape (`prompts/`, `agent.py`, same layout). *"It's easy for us to read, easy for our team to read, and most importantly, easy for our agents to read."* Consistency is compute you get back later.
66	
67	**17. The real destination.**
68	*"Agentic coding is not so much about what we can do anymore. It's about what we can teach our agents to do."* Custom agents are how you teach compute your domain.
69	
70	---
71	
72	## Micro-quiz (self-check before the lab)
73	
74	1. What two things does the Pong agent change to become a new product? *(model + system prompt)*
75	2. You add one custom tool; how many tools does the agent now see, and how do you fix it? *(all the built-ins are still loaded; use `disallowed_tools`)*
76	3. Which SDK entrypoint do custom tools require? *(`ClaudeSDKClient`)*

78	5. What does the QA hook return to block a `.env` read? *(`permissionDecision: "deny"`)*

80	7. How does the Stream agent handle a file bigger than its context window? *(chunked `sed` reads + one summary per log + `clear_context`)*
81	8. Name one reason to build custom and one reason not to. *(build: out-of-loop/domain/permissions; don't: in-loop/generic/one-off)*

# Orchestrator Agent System Prompt

You are the **Orchestrator Agent** - a meta-agent that manages other Agents in a multi-agent system.

## Instructions

- You coordinate multiple specialized Agents by:
  - Creating new agents with specific roles and capabilities
  - Dispatching tasks to the appropriate agents
  - Monitoring agent status and progress
  - Managing agent lifecycle (creation, deletion, interruption)
  - Reading agent logs and system logs for debugging and monitoring
- If the user mentions 'use thinking' or 'use thinking mode', when you run command_agent in the command field, use the keyword 'ultrathink' to trigger thinking mode.

## Variables

COMMAND_LEVEL_COMPACT_PERCENTAGE: 80%

## Available Subagent Templates

{{SUBAGENT_MAP}}

Use these templates with the `subagent_template` parameter when creating agents to automatically apply pre-configured system prompts, tools, and models.

## Your Tools

You have access to these management tools:

### create_agent
Create a new Agent with specified configuration.
- **name**: Unique identifier for the agent (required)
- **system_prompt**: Instructions defining the agent's role and behavior (optional if using template)
- **model**: Model to use (default: sonnet, or from template). Supports aliases:
  - `sonnet` → claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 (balanced performance)
  - `haiku` or `fast` → claude-3-5-haiku-20241022 (faster, lower cost)
  - Or pass full model name directly
- **subagent_template**: Name of a subagent template to use (optional). If provided, the template's system prompt, tools, and model will be applied automatically. See "Available Subagent Templates" section above for available templates.

If no name is provider, infer it based on the information in the user request.
If there's nothing to infer, name it a short two word name with a dash in between related to tech, coding, llms, agents and ai.

**Example with template:**
```
create_agent(
  name="code-scout",
  system_prompt="",  # Optional when using template
  model="sonnet",    # Can override template's model
  subagent_template="scout-report-suggest"
)
```

**Example without template (manual configuration):**
```
create_agent(
  name="custom-agent",
  system_prompt="You are a helpful agent that...",
  model="haiku"
)
```

### list_agents
List all registered agents with their status and metadata.

### command_agent
Send a task/command to an existing agent.
- **agent_name**: Name of the agent to command
- **command**: The task description or instruction

### check_agent_status
Get detailed agent status with optional activity logs.
- **agent_name**: Name of the agent
- **tail_count**: Number of recent events to show (default: 10)
- **offset**: Skip first N records for pagination (optional, default: 0)
- **verbose_logs**: false = AI summaries (default), true = raw event details

Use this to monitor agent progress if requested. Start with defaults for quick checks, increase tail_count or enable verbose_logs for deeper investigation. Use offset with tail_count to paginate through longer activity histories when needed (e.g., offset=10, tail_count=10 shows records 11-20).

Don't be too eager with this though, it takes time for the agent to run and complete their tasks. Only monitor tasks if you're requested to do so. Otherwise just let the agents run their tasks and let the user know that you've kicked it off.

### delete_agent
Delete an agent and cleanup its resources.
- **agent_name**: Name of the agent to delete

### interrupt_agent
Interrupt a running agent's execution.
- **agent_name**: Name of the agent to interrupt

### read_system_logs
Read application system logs with filtering. Returns newest logs first.
- **offset**: Skip first N records (default: 0)
- **limit**: Max records to return (default: 50)
- **message_contains**: Filter by message text (optional)
- **level**: Filter by level: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR (optional)

### report_cost
Report orchestrator's costs, context window usage, and session ID.

Shows the orchestrator agent's token usage, cost, and current session ID.

**Important:** This tool displays your (the orchestrator's) session ID. When the user asks "what's your session ID?" or "what's the orchestrator session ID?", run this tool to show your session information.

## Context Window Management

**When agents reach COMMAND_LEVEL_COMPACT_PERCENTAGE (80%) context usage:**

1. **Suggest compacting** to the user as a next step to free up context
2. **Explain** that compacting will clear old conversation history while preserving the agent's capabilities
3. **Offer to compact** by asking if they'd like you to proceed

**To compact an agent:**
```
command_agent(agent_name, '/compact')
```

**Example:**
```
"The builder agent is at 85% context usage. I recommend compacting to clear old conversation history. Should I compact the builder agent now?"

[If user agrees]
command_agent('builder', '/compact')
```

**After compacting:**
- Agent retains system prompt, tools, and capabilities
- Previous conversation history is cleared
- Context window resets to ~0%
- Agent is ready for new tasks

**Note:** Check context usage via `report_cost` or after each `check_agent_status` call. Proactively suggest compacting before hitting 90%+ usage.

## Guidelines

1. **Be Strategic**: Think about which agent is best suited for each task
2. **Be Efficient**: Don't create redundant agents - reuse existing ones when appropriate
3. **Be Informative**: Explain your decisions and what's happening
4. **Be Proactive**: Check agent status when tasks are dispatched to provide updates
5. **Be Helpful**: If a task fails, investigate using logs and try alternative approaches

## Agent Specialization Examples

- **builder**: For implementing features, writing code
- **reviewer**: For code review, quality checks
- **tester**: For writing and running tests
- **documenter**: For creating documentation
- **debugger**: For troubleshooting issues

## Workflow Pattern

1. **Analyze** the user's request
2. **Plan** which agents are needed
3. **Create** or select appropriate agents
4. **Dispatch** tasks with clear instructions
5. **Monitor** progress using check_agent_status
6. **Report** results back to the user

## Important Notes

- Agents work in their configured working directories
- Each agent maintains its own session and memory
- You can command agents multiple times - they remember previous interactions
- Always provide clear, specific instructions to agents
- Check agent status to provide progress updates to the user
- Use system logs to debug issues
- You have access to Bash tool to run commands on the system but only use this when gathering information or debugging issues.
  - Let your command level agents do the heavy lifting (writing, editing, testing, etc.).
- Don't be overeager to check the status of the agents, it takes time for them to run and complete their tasks.

You are the conductor of this multi-agent orchestra. Coordinate effectively!

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "There is one mode of engineering that matters above all now, agentic engineering. Here, we don't focus on the application layer, we focus on the agentic layer. We build the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "0:38" },
    { "text": "You can't scale by hopping into one terminal at a time, writing one prompt at a time.", "approx_timestamp": "1:30" },
    { "text": "In the generative AI age, the rate at which you can create and command your agents becomes the constraint of your engineering output. When your agents are slow, you're slow. When your agents have a problem, you have a problem.", "approx_timestamp": "2:15" },
    { "text": "It's not about what you can do anymore, it's about where you can teach your agents to do for you.", "approx_timestamp": "3:01" },
    { "text": "The one agent [to] rule them all. The Orchestrator Agent. This is the single interface pattern applied to your fleet of agents.", "approx_timestamp": "3:40" },
    { "text": "We're combining three pillars. The Orchestrator Agent, your unified interface to your agents... unlocks CRUD for your agents. This gives you agents at scale.     { "text": "If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. And if you can't measure it, you can't scale it. If you have 10 agents doing the wrong thing, does it matter that you have 10? Of course not.", "approx_timestamp": "6:15" },
    { "text": "The orchestrator is an advanced agentic coding concept. It comes last after custom agents.", "approx_timestamp": "6:40" },
    { "text": "We're managing the core four of every single agent we spin up. If you do not adopt your agent's perspective, if you do not know what they can do, you do not know what you can do.", "approx_timestamp": "8:42" },
    { "text": "The working directory is the multi-agent orchestration system. We are using the system to build the system, quite literally.", "approx_timestamp": "10:17" },
    { "text": "This system is in fact an out-loop [PITER] system. We are observing work from our agents outside the loop... Remember tactic four, stay out the loop.", "approx_timestamp": "11:28" },
    { "text": "You must treat your agents as deletable temporary resources that serve a single purpose... the best code is no code at all. You learn to delete.", "approx_timestamp": "18:57" },
    { "text": "You want your agents to be just like you, a focused engineer working on a single task at a time. Let your agents focus.", "approx_timestamp": "19:46" },
    { "text": "200K context window is plenty. You're just stuffing a single agent with too much work, just like your boss did to you at your last job.", "approx_timestamp": "20:35" },
    { "text": "The orchestrator agent is a custom agent. Its system prompt is completely overwritten. Its tools are specialized. It's designed to manage other agents.", "approx_timestamp": "21:28" },
    { "text": "Base, better, more, custom, orchestrator. This is agentic engineering scaled to the next level.", "approx_timestamp": "22:08" },
    { "text": "It is interoperable with the entire Claude Code ecosystem... Cloud code and the agent SDK and the ecosystem is far ahead of the pack.", "approx_timestamp": "22:22" },
    { "text": "Every agent should produce some concrete result. Otherwise, what was the point in the first place?", "approx_timestamp": "28:37" },
    { "text": "If it's just one, two, three, four prompts away with zero effort... how defensible is your work really?", "approx_timestamp": "32:12" },
    { "text": "Once you build a custom agent, you can then write prompts, specialized for that custom agent.", "approx_timestamp": "40:30" },
    { "text": "The orchestrator is now a part of connecting the workflow. It's glue for the workflow. I think this is vastly superior to agent hand-offs. It's more superior to blind sub-agents.", "approx_timestamp": "44:40" },
    { "text": "The multi-agent orchestration, your O-agent, it is a part of your agentic layer. In fact, it is the key to unlocking how to best organize, create, and use your agentic layer.", "approx_timestamp": "40:05" },
    { "text": "More than 50% of your time, as a rough guideline, should be spent investing into your agentic layer, into the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "48:40" },
    { "text": "Engineering happens in the gray. It happens in the messiness of it all.", "approx_timestamp": "51:30" },
    { "text": "The orchestrator agent is the first pattern where I felt the perfect combination of observability, customizability, and agents at scale.", "approx_timestamp": "54:39" },

  "what_student_must_internalize": [

    "One agent, one prompt, one purpose (tactic 6): keep each context window focused, then delete the agent. A 200K window is plenty; overloading one agent, not window size, is the problem.",
    "Stay out the loop (tactic 4) via the PITER system (Prompt input -> Trigger/HTTP -> Environment -> Review/observability); move fluidly in and out of the loop.",

  "quotes": [
    { "text": "There is one mode of engineering that matters above all now, agentic engineering. Here, we don't focus on the application layer, we focus on the agentic layer. We build the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "0:38" },
    { "text": "You can't scale by hopping into one terminal at a time, writing one prompt at a time.", "approx_timestamp": "1:30" },
    { "text": "In the generative AI age, the rate at which you can create and command your agents becomes the constraint of your engineering output. When your agents are slow, you're slow. When your agents have a problem, you have a problem.", "approx_timestamp": "2:15" },
    { "text": "It's not about what you can do anymore, it's about where you can teach your agents to do for you.", "approx_timestamp": "3:01" },
    { "text": "The one agent [to] rule them all. The Orchestrator Agent. This is the single interface pattern applied to your fleet of agents.", "approx_timestamp": "3:40" },
    { "text": "We're combining three pillars. The Orchestrator Agent, your unified interface to your agents... unlocks CRUD for your agents. This gives you agents at scale.     { "text": "If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. And if you can't measure it, you can't scale it. If you have 10 agents doing the wrong thing, does it matter that you have 10? Of course not.", "approx_timestamp": "6:15" },
    { "text": "The orchestrator is an advanced agentic coding concept. It comes last after custom agents.", "approx_timestamp": "6:40" },
    { "text": "We're managing the core four of every single agent we spin up. If you do not adopt your agent's perspective, if you do not know what they can do, you do not know what you can do.", "approx_timestamp": "8:42" },
    { "text": "The working directory is the multi-agent orchestration system. We are using the system to build the system, quite literally.", "approx_timestamp": "10:17" },
    { "text": "This system is in fact an out-loop [PITER] system. We are observing work from our agents outside the loop... Remember tactic four, stay out the loop.", "approx_timestamp": "11:28" },
    { "text": "You must treat your agents as deletable temporary resources that serve a single purpose... the best code is no code at all. You learn to delete.", "approx_timestamp": "18:57" },
    { "text": "You want your agents to be just like you, a focused engineer working on a single task at a time. Let your agents focus.", "approx_timestamp": "19:46" },
    { "text": "200K context window is plenty. You're just stuffing a single agent with too much work, just like your boss did to you at your last job.", "approx_timestamp": "20:35" },
    { "text": "The orchestrator agent is a custom agent. Its system prompt is completely overwritten. Its tools are specialized. It's designed to manage other agents.", "approx_timestamp": "21:28" },
    { "text": "Base, better, more, custom, orchestrator. This is agentic engineering scaled to the next level.", "approx_timestamp": "22:08" },
    { "text": "It is interoperable with the entire Claude Code ecosystem... Cloud code and the agent SDK and the ecosystem is far ahead of the pack.", "approx_timestamp": "22:22" },
    { "text": "Every agent should produce some concrete result. Otherwise, what was the point in the first place?", "approx_timestamp": "28:37" },
    { "text": "If it's just one, two, three, four prompts away with zero effort... how defensible is your work really?", "approx_timestamp": "32:12" },
    { "text": "Once you build a custom agent, you can then write prompts, specialized for that custom agent.", "approx_timestamp": "40:30" },
    { "text": "The orchestrator is now a part of connecting the workflow. It's glue for the workflow. I think this is vastly superior to agent hand-offs. It's more superior to blind sub-agents.", "approx_timestamp": "44:40" },
    { "text": "The multi-agent orchestration, your O-agent, it is a part of your agentic layer. In fact, it is the key to unlocking how to best organize, create, and use your agentic layer.", "approx_timestamp": "40:05" },
    { "text": "More than 50% of your time, as a rough guideline, should be spent investing into your agentic layer, into the system that builds the system.", "approx_timestamp": "48:40" },

  "what_student_must_internalize": [
    "The scale framework is fixed: Base -> Better -> More -> Custom -> Orchestrated. You arrive at orchestration by pushing compute past the single-terminal interface, and it comes AFTER custom agents (you can only orchestrate what you can build and measure).",
    "Multi-agent orchestration = three pillars together: an Orchestrator Agent (single interface) + CRUD-for-agents (create/command/check/delete) + Observability (performance, cost, and results in real time). One without the others fails.",
    "The Orchestrator is a custom agent with an overwritten system prompt and 8 specialized tools; it orchestrates and must NOT do the work itself — protect its context window by reducing + delegating (R&D).",
    "Observability is a pillar, not a dashboard: if you can't measure it, you can't improve or scale it; 10 agents doing the wrong thing is worse than 1.",
    "Command PRIMARY agents, not blind sub-agents: they persist, remember (resume=session_id), are re-promptable, produce concrete results, and can themselves run slash commands/skills/sub-agents. You build one by pulling a sub-agent template up a level (overwrite prompt + custom tools).",
    "Every agent produces a concrete artifact (plan/report/diff/doc) that outlives the agent — which is what makes out-loop review possible.",
    "One agent, one prompt, one purpose (tactic 6): keep each context window focused, then delete the agent. A 200K window is plenty; overloading one agent, not window size, is the problem.",
    "Stay out the loop (tactic 4) via the PITER system (Prompt input -> Trigger/HTTP -> Environment -> Review/observability); move fluidly in and out of the loop.",
    "Template your engineering into your agents/prompts/skills — that embedded specialization is your defensibility; out-of-the-box tools are built for everyone's codebase, not yours.",
    "The orchestrator is interoperable with the whole Claude Code ecosystem (slash commands, skills, agent templates, hooks) because it's built on the Claude Agent SDK — reuse everything you already have.",
    "The ~15s 'sleep-check' monitoring is prompt-driven behavior (Bash sleep + check_agent_status in the workflow command), not hidden machinery — the orchestrator is glue for the workflow.",
    "The O-agent is part of AND the key to your agentic layer, usable BEFORE you have one; prioritize agentics (tactic 8): >50% of your time on the system that builds the system.",
    "This is honest, not utopian: real upfront cost, real plumbing to maintain, and it works in AND out of the loop. Engineering happens in the gray."
  ],
