# AH-4 — Multi-Agent Orchestration: The O-Agent — Master Teaching Notes

**Lesson:** Agentic Horizon #4 (course order 12, Advanced) · **Runtime:** 56:08 · **Codebase:** `agentic-horizon/multi-agent-orchestration`
**Tactic:** *Orchestrate Your Agents* — put one custom Orchestrator Agent in front of your whole fleet, give it CRUD-for-agents + observability, and command agents at scale through a single interface.

> One-sentence spine: *You've scaled better → more → custom agents; the interface itself is now your bottleneck, so you build **one agent to rule them all** — the Orchestrator — and combine three pillars (Orchestrator + CRUD-for-agents + Observability) to command a fleet out of the loop.*

Every major idea below is built for a struggling learner: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name → Failure → Retrieval.**

---

## 0. The frame that anchors everything

The lesson is one continuous screen recording of a **custom dark-theme web app** (`MULTI-AGENT ORCHESTRATION`, `127.0.0.1:5175`) with three columns: **AgentList** (left, per-agent cards) · **EventStream** (center, filterable logs) · **OrchestratorChat** (right, the O-agent). A **Cmd+K palette** exposes the whole capability surface. Keep the [architecture frame `t0636`] and the [capability palette `t0300`] open while you read — between them they show *what the system is* and *what it can do*.

---

## 1. Multi-agent orchestration is the next rung — because the interface is the wall

- **Hook.** You got better agents, then more agents, then custom agents. So why do you still feel slow? Because *"you can't scale by hopping into one terminal at a time, writing one prompt at a time."*
- **Picture.** A ladder: **Base → Better → More → Custom → Orchestrated.** Each rung: *"scale your compute to scale your impact."* You're stuck one rung too low — running agents by hand.
- **Worked example.** In the generative-AI age, *"the rate at which you can create and command your agents becomes the constraint of your engineering output. When your agents are slow, you're slow. When your agents have a problem, you have a problem."* One human clicking between terminals cannot command a fleet.
- **Name it.** **The agent-scale framework**, and the new top rung: **Multi-Agent Orchestration.** It is *"an advanced agentic coding concept. It comes last after custom agents"* — you can only orchestrate what you can already build (custom) and measure (observability).
- **Failure to avoid.** Scaling agent *count* without an interface — opening 10 tabs. *"If you have 10 agents doing the wrong thing, does it matter that you have 10? Of course not."*
- **Retrieval.** *Recite the five rungs. Why does orchestration come last?* (Base→Better→More→Custom→Orchestrated; you can't orchestrate what you can't build or measure.)

---

## 2. The Orchestrator Agent (O-agent): the single interface pattern, applied to agents

- **Hook.** *Where is our input field?* This isn't an app for normal users; it's for the agentic engineer. You talk to exactly **one** agent — and it commands all the others.
- **Picture.** [Frame `t0258`]: the empty shell, three title cards fading in — **AGENT ORCHESTRATION / OBSERVABILITY / AGENTS AT SCALE** — and a right panel: *"Start a conversation — Ask the orchestrator to create, manage, or command agents."*
- **Worked example.** The orchestrator is a **custom agent**: its system prompt is *fully overwritten* — verbatim in `orchestrator_agent_system_prompt.md`: *"You are the **Orchestrator Agent** — a meta-agent that manages other Agents in a multi-agent system."* Its tools are **8 specialized management tools** (an in-memory MCP server), not the Claude Code engineering toolset. You say *"create three agents to summarize the codebase…"* → it emits **6 tool calls** (3× `create_agent` + 3× `command_agent`) and the fleet does the work.
- **Name it.** **The single interface pattern** — *"an existing engineering paradigm that great engineers have used for decades,"* now pointed at agents. The **O-agent** / **OA**.
- **Failure to avoid.** Letting the orchestrator do the engineering. It must not: *"we don't want our orchestrator agent getting involved in the actual work. It is just here to orchestrate."*
- **Retrieval.** *What kind of agent is the orchestrator, and what does it deliberately NOT do?* (A custom agent, system prompt overwritten, 8 tools; it orchestrates — it never does the heavy lifting, so its context stays tiny.)

---

## 3. The three pillars: Orchestrator + CRUD-for-agents + Observability

- **Hook.** *"But it's not just the Orchestrator Agent that matters. We're combining three pillars."*
- **Picture.** Three cards over the empty UI (`t0258`): **Orchestrator Agent** (unified interface) · **CRUD** for agents (agents at scale) · **Observability** (performance, cost, results).
- **Worked example.** Fire one prompt → three agents appear in the left rail, each with a live status, model, cost, and context bar; the center EventStream shows every response/tool/thinking/hook; the right panel shows the orchestrator's dispatch summary. That's all three pillars in one screen ([`t0402`]).
- **Name it.** **The three pillars of multi-agent orchestration.** *"When you combine these three, you get a powerful solution… This is you controlling your compute at scale."*
- **Failure to avoid.** Treating observability as a nice dashboard, or forgetting CRUD. Drop a pillar and you either fly blind or can't manage the fleet.
- **Retrieval.** *Name the three pillars and what each unlocks.* (Orchestrator = single interface; CRUD = agents at scale; Observability = control at scale.)

---

## 4. Observability is key — *measure it or you can't scale it*

- **Hook.** Why build a whole observability UI instead of just reading terminal output? *"Observability is a key component of a successful multi-agent system."*
- **Picture.** [`t0690`] the Consumed-vs-Produced ledger with inline **Show Diff** and an **Export File Activity** button; filter tabs **RESPONSE / TOOL / THINKING / HOOK**; per-agent chips; regex search; Auto-Follow.
- **Worked example.** *"If something went wrong, I could dial in right here and understand why, when, and where, and who. What agent messed up? Was it our planner? Was it our builder?"* You can one-click into any produced file and read the diff — in the loop only as long as you need.
- **Name it.** **Observability as a pillar** — *"If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. And if you can't measure it, you can't scale it."*
- **Failure to avoid.** Ten agents doing the wrong thing feels productive and isn't. Without measurement you can't tell.
- **Retrieval.** *Complete the couplet and give the pipeline.* ("can't measure → can't improve/scale"; SDK/hook event → Postgres (`agent_logs`) → WebSocket → Pinia store → UI, + a Haiku one-sentence summary.)

---

## 5. Primary agents, not sub-agents (the differentiator)

- **Hook.** Every engineer's first objection: *"Aren't these just sub-agents? Why aren't you just using sub-agents?"*
- **Picture.** An agent card that stays put with a template badge, a running cost, and a re-promptable session — versus a Task sub-agent that fires once and vanishes.
- **Worked example.** *"Instead of just using a sub-agent here, we can turn this into a full-on primary agent by blowing away the system prompt and by giving it custom tools… You can't do all this with a sub-agent. You're locked in, it's too narrow."* In code: `create_agent(subagent_template="scout-report-suggest-fast")` resolves the `.claude/agents/*.md` template into a **fresh `ClaudeSDKClient`** (its own session), and `command_agent` re-mounts it with `resume=session_id` so it remembers.
- **Name it.** **Primary agents** (re-promptable, persistent, produce results, can themselves run slash commands/skills/sub-agents) vs **sub-agents** (ephemeral, narrow, context blown away). Building one = **pull a sub-agent template up a level** (overwrite prompt + custom tools).
- **Failure to avoid.** Dismissing the whole system as "just sub-agents" and missing what persistence + re-prompting + concrete results buys you.
- **Retrieval.** *Give two concrete things a primary agent can do that a Task sub-agent can't.* (Be re-commanded with memory via `resume=`; run its own slash commands/skills/sub-agents; produce an inspectable artifact you keep.)

---

## 6. Manage the core four of every agent — and protect the orchestrator's context (R&D)

- **Hook.** All the UI, all the features — what are you actually looking at? *"It's all just the core four."*
- **Picture.** [`t0528`] the **CONTEXT / MODEL / PROMPT / TOOLS** Venn over the live per-agent cards (context bar `x/200k`, model badge, cost).
- **Worked example.** *"We're managing the core four of every single agent we spin up. If you do not adopt your agent's perspective… you do not know what you can do."* The orchestrator keeps *its own* context minimal by **Reducing** and **Delegating** (the R&D framework from AH-1): *"it is not always observing the logs. It cannot be. We have to protect its context window."* Even after conducting huge work, the orchestrator card shows ~4–41k/200k because context is reduced + delegated.
- **Name it.** **Core four at scale** + **R&D (Reduce & Delegate)**. The system prompt even sets `COMMAND_LEVEL_COMPACT_PERCENTAGE: 80%` — at ~80% it suggests `command_agent(agent, '/compact')`.
- **Failure to avoid.** Making the orchestrator read every agent log to "stay informed" — that blows up the one context window you most need thin.
- **Retrieval.** *Why does the orchestrator's context window stay small? Which two R&D verbs?* (It never does the work or reads all logs — it Reduces its own context and Delegates to focused agents.)

---

## 7. Stay out the loop — the PITER system (tactic 4)

- **Hook.** *"This is quite literally a prompt input…"* Why a database and WebSockets instead of a chat window?
- **Picture.** A 4-stage out-loop pipeline: **P**rompt input → **T**rigger (HTTP) → **E**nvironment → **R**eview (observability). (Render as a diagram; see frame-plan `unframed_beats`.)
- **Worked example.** Prompt = your Cmd+K message (`POST /send_chat`). Trigger = the HTTP request to the FastAPI server (fired as a background task). Environment = the working directory the agents operate in (here, the app's own codebase — *"we are using the system to build the system"*). Review = observability. *"We are observing work from our agents outside the loop… Remember tactic four, stay out the loop."*
- **Name it.** **PITER** (out-loop system). ⚠️ The auto-transcript renders it **"Peter"**; the loot-box notes spell it out; it is **not** a string in the repo — it's a lesson concept mapped onto real mechanics.
- **Failure to avoid.** Reading "out of the loop" as "unsupervised and hoping." The **R** is Review — you still inspect results; you just don't type back-and-forth prompts.
- **Retrieval.** *Expand PITER and name the tactic.* (Prompt input → Trigger (HTTP) → Environment → Review; tactic 4, stay out the loop.)

---

## 8. One agent, one prompt, one purpose — then delete (tactic 6)

- **Hook.** *"There's a journey every engineer goes through… you learn that the best code is no code at all. You learn to delete."*
- **Picture.** [`t1143`] three `delete_agent{agent_name}` calls, then **"✅ All agents deleted successfully!"** — the fleet cleared, ready for the next task.
- **Worked example.** Focus each agent on a single task with a protected window, let it produce its result, then delete it. *"You must treat your agents as deletable temporary resources that serve a single purpose."* A 200K window is plenty — *"you're just stuffing a single agent with too much work, just like your boss did to you at your last job."* Sidesteps context rot / pollution / toxic context.
- **Name it.** **One agent, one prompt, one purpose** (TAC lesson 6, *Let Your Agents Focus*).
- **Failure to avoid.** Hoarding stale, context-polluted agents. The *produced artifacts* persist; the agent is disposable — *"let the agents go home… delete it, back to the data center."*
- **Retrieval.** *State the three-word rule and the 200K claim.* (One agent, one prompt, one purpose; 200K is plenty — overloading one agent, not window size, is the problem.)

---

## 9. Every agent produces a concrete result — and you template YOUR engineering into it

- **Hook.** *"Every agent should produce some concrete result. Otherwise, what was the point in the first place?"*
- **Picture.** [`t2148`] a **✅ Scout Report Complete** with a produced `app_docs/header-pills-scout-report.md (+363)` and its consumed files — a durable artifact you can review after the agent is gone.
- **Worked example.** The scout agent reports in *your* dedicated structure because you **templated your engineering** into its system prompt. *"We've templated our engineering… a dedicated scout report, a dedicated structure."* That embedded specialization is your **defensibility**: *"If it's just one, two, three, four prompts away with zero effort… how defensible is your work really?"* Out-of-the-box tools are built for everyone's codebase, not yours.
- **Name it.** **Results-oriented engineering** + **templating your engineering** (the moat).
- **Failure to avoid.** Shipping the orchestrator app with none of *your* specialized prompts/tools/agents inside it — an undifferentiated tool with no edge.
- **Retrieval.** *Why must every agent produce an artifact, and where does defensibility come from?* (So work is inspectable/handed-off and outlives the agent; defensibility comes from the specialized engineering you template in, not the app shell.)

---

## 10. The orchestrator is glue — ecosystem interop + orchestration prompts (ADWs)

- **Hook.** *"It is interoperable with the entire Claude Code ecosystem."*
- **Picture.** [`t1445`] the orchestrator spins up a `codebase-questioner` (Haiku) and commands it to run **`/question`** → *"Yes, both your orchestrator and agents can use Skills."* A **`/prime`** is mid-type. Slash commands, skills, agent templates, hooks — all plug in.
- **Worked example.** Because you can specialize prompts for a custom agent, you get **orchestration prompts**: `/orch_plan_w_scouts_build_review` is a **plan → build → review → report** three-phase **ADW**. [`t2625`] all three agents up front — a *dynamic* planner (custom prompt, no template), a `build-agent` builder, a `review-agent` reviewer; the planner consumes real Vue files and produces `specs/responsive-ui-plan.md`. The orchestrator is the **glue**: *"I think this is vastly superior to agent hand-offs… more superior to blind sub-agents."* Its **sleep-check** monitoring — [`t3215`] `Bash{command:"sleep 20"}` + `check_agent_status` — is **prompt-driven** (the workflow file sets `SLEEP_INTERVAL: 15 seconds`), *not* hidden Python.
- **Name it.** **Ecosystem interoperability** + **orchestration prompts / ADWs** + **the orchestrator as glue** (the sleep-check loop).
- **Failure to avoid.** Assuming the ~15s monitor is machinery you can't change. It lives in the workflow command — read it, edit it.
- **Retrieval.** *What are the three phases of the demo workflow, and how does the ~15s loop work?* (Plan → Build → Review (+ report); the orchestrator runs Bash(sleep 15) + check_agent_status until a `response` is followed by a `hook` `Stop`.)

---

## 11. The agentic layer, prioritize agentics (tactic 8), and operating in the gray

- **Hook.** *"Make no mistake, the multi-agent orchestration, your O-agent, it is a part of your agentic layer."*
- **Picture.** The O-agent as both a piece of the agentic layer **and** *"the key to unlocking how to best organize, create, and use your agentic layer"* — usable **before** you have a full layer.
- **Worked example.** Prioritize agentics (TAC lesson 8): *"More than 50% of your time, as a rough guideline, should be spent investing into your agentic layer, into the system that builds the system."* But be honest — this costs upfront investment and ongoing maintenance (orchestrator, Postgres, WebSockets): *"another piece of your agentic layer you'll have to maintain."* And the big missing piece is deterministic **AI Developer Workflows**: *"How does this plug into deterministic code?… We're missing our AI developer workflows. This is the big missing piece."*
- **Name it.** **Prioritize agentics** + **operating in the gray**. *"Engineering happens in the gray. It happens in the messiness of it all."*
- **Failure to avoid.** Waiting for a "finished" out-loop utopia, or selling one. Dan explicitly refuses that: it works in **and** out of the loop, and you step between modes.
- **Retrieval.** *What's the >50% guideline, and the single biggest missing piece?* (Spend >50% of your time on the agentic layer; the missing piece is deterministic-code / ADW integration — a future lesson.)

---

## The fleet at a glance

**The 8 orchestrator (management) tools — the "CRUD":**

| Tool | CRUD | Signature (verified in `agent_manager.py` + palette frame `t0300`) |
|---|---|---|
| `create_agent` | **C** | `create_agent(name, system_prompt?, model?, subagent_template?)` |
| `list_agents` | R | `list_agents()` |
| `command_agent` | C-task / **U** | `command_agent(agent_name, command)` — also `/compact` at 80% |
| `check_agent_status` | R | `check_agent_status(agent_name, tail_count=10, offset=0, verbose_logs=false)` — the sleep-check poll |
| `delete_agent` | **D** | `delete_agent(agent_name)` |
| `interrupt_agent` | D/U | `interrupt_agent(agent_name)` |
| `read_system_logs` | R | `read_system_logs(offset=0, limit=50, message_contains?, level?)` |
| `report_cost` | R | `report_cost()` — orchestrator tokens/cost/context%/session id |

**The agent templates (`.claude/agents/*.md`):**

| Template | Model | Tools | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scout-report-suggest-fast` | Haiku | Read, Glob, Grep | read-only "scout fast" → SCOUT REPORT (demoed by name) |
| `scout-report-suggest` | Sonnet | Read, Glob, Grep | deeper read-only scout |
| `build-agent` | Sonnet | Write, Read, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash, TodoWrite | implement one file from a spec (the builder) |
| `review-agent` | Sonnet | Write, Read, Bash, Grep, Glob | diff-review → Blocker/High/Med/Low → PASS/FAIL |
| `meta-agent` | Opus | Write, WebFetch, firecrawl, MultiEdit | agent architect (generates sub-agents) |
| `docs-scraper` | Haiku | firecrawl, WebFetch, Write, Edit | scrape URL → `ai_docs/` markdown |
| `playwright-validator` | Sonnet | 19× `mcp__playwright__browser_*` + Write/Edit | drive browser, screenshot, validate |

*The **planner** has no static template — it's created dynamically (custom prompt, no template) by the plan→build→review workflow. Frame `t2625` shows the planner card with no template badge.*

**Models (from `config.py`):** Sonnet `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` (orchestrator + primary/build/review) · Haiku `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` (scouts, docs-scraper, AI summaries) · Opus (meta-agent). On-screen badges: **SONNET-4.5 / HAIKU-4.5**.

## Glossary

- **O-agent / OA / Orchestrator Agent** — the single custom agent that manages the fleet; system prompt overwritten; 8 management tools.
- **Single interface pattern** — one interface in front of many; here, one agent commanding a fleet.
- **Three pillars** — Orchestrator + CRUD-for-agents + Observability.
- **CRUD for agents** — create/command(+read status)/update/delete over agents.
- **Primary agent** — a persistent, re-promptable spawned `ClaudeSDKClient` (own session), vs an ephemeral Task **sub-agent**.
- **Agent template** — a `.claude/agents/*.md` sub-agent definition resolved into a primary agent via `create_agent(subagent_template=...)`.
- **PITER** — out-loop system: Prompt input → Trigger (HTTP) → Environment → Review (observability). *(Transcribed "Peter"; not in the repo.)*
- **Sleep-check loop** — prompt-driven `Bash(sleep 15)` + `check_agent_status` monitoring in the workflow commands.
- **ADW** — AI Developer Workflow (plan → build → review → report), here as an orchestration prompt.
- **R&D framework** — Reduce (context) & Delegate (work) — from AH-1.
- **Consumed vs Produced** — files an agent Read vs Wrote/Edited (via `file_tracker.py`), shown with inline diffs.

# AH-4 — Multi-Agent Orchestration: The O-Agent — Master Teaching Notes

**Lesson:** Agentic Horizon #4 (course order 12, Advanced) · **Runtime:** 56:08 · **Codebase:** `agentic-horizon/multi-agent-orchestration`
**Tactic:** *Orchestrate Your Agents* — put one custom Orchestrator Agent in front of your whole fleet, give it CRUD-for-agents + observability, and command agents at scale through a single interface.

> One-sentence spine: *You've scaled better → more → custom agents; the interface itself is now your bottleneck, so you build **one agent to rule them all** — the Orchestrator — and combine three pillars (Orchestrator + CRUD-for-agents + Observability) to command a fleet out of the loop.*

Every major idea below is built for a struggling learner: **Hook → Picture → Worked example → Name → Failure → Retrieval.**

---

## 0. The frame that anchors everything

The lesson is one continuous screen recording of a **custom dark-theme web app** (`MULTI-AGENT ORCHESTRATION`, `127.0.0.1:5175`) with three columns: **AgentList** (left, per-agent cards) · **EventStream** (center, filterable logs) · **OrchestratorChat** (right, the O-agent). A **Cmd+K palette** exposes the whole capability surface. Keep the [architecture frame `t0636`] and the [capability palette `t0300`] open while you read — between them they show *what the system is* and *what it can do*.

---

## 1. Multi-agent orchestration is the next rung — because the interface is the wall

- **Hook.** You got better agents, then more agents, then custom agents. So why do you still feel slow? Because *"you can't scale by hopping into one terminal at a time, writing one prompt at a time."*
- **Picture.** A ladder: **Base → Better → More → Custom → Orchestrated.** Each rung: *"scale your compute to scale your impact."* You're stuck one rung too low — running agents by hand.
- **Worked example.** In the generative-AI age, *"the rate at which you can create and command your agents becomes the constraint of your engineering output. When your agents are slow, you're slow. When your agents have a problem, you have a problem."* One human clicking between terminals cannot command a fleet.
- **Name it.** **The agent-scale framework**, and the new top rung: **Multi-Agent Orchestration.** It is *"an advanced agentic coding concept. It comes last after custom agents"* — you can only orchestrate what you can already build (custom) and measure (observability).
- **Failure to avoid.** Scaling agent *count* without an interface — opening 10 tabs. *"If you have 10 agents doing the wrong thing, does it matter that you have 10? Of course not."*
- **Retrieval.** *Recite the five rungs. Why does orchestration come last?* (Base→Better→More→Custom→Orchestrated; you can't orchestrate what you can't build or measure.)

---

## 2. The Orchestrator Agent (O-agent): the single interface pattern, applied to agents

- **Hook.** *Where is our input field?* This isn't an app for normal users; it's for the agentic engineer. You talk to exactly **one** agent — and it commands all the others.
- **Picture.** [Frame `t0258`]: the empty shell, three title cards fading in — **AGENT ORCHESTRATION / OBSERVABILITY / AGENTS AT SCALE** — and a right panel: *"Start a conversation — Ask the orchestrator to create, manage, or command agents."*
- **Worked example.** The orchestrator is a **custom agent**: its system prompt is *fully overwritten* — verbatim in `orchestrator_agent_system_prompt.md`: *"You are the **Orchestrator Agent** — a meta-agent that manages other Agents in a multi-agent system."* Its tools are **8 specialized management tools** (an in-memory MCP server), not the Claude Code engineering toolset. You say *"create three agents to summarize the codebase…"* → it emits **6 tool calls** (3× `create_agent` + 3× `command_agent`) and the fleet does the work.
- **Name it.** **The single interface pattern** — *"an existing engineering paradigm that great engineers have used for decades,"* now pointed at agents. The **O-agent** / **OA**.
- **Failure to avoid.** Letting the orchestrator do the engineering. It must not: *"we don't want our orchestrator agent getting involved in the actual work. It is just here to orchestrate."*
- **Retrieval.** *What kind of agent is the orchestrator, and what does it deliberately NOT do?* (A custom agent, system prompt overwritten, 8 tools; it orchestrates — it never does the heavy lifting, so its context stays tiny.)

---

## 3. The three pillars: Orchestrator + CRUD-for-agents + Observability

- **Hook.** *"But it's not just the Orchestrator Agent that matters. We're combining three pillars."*
- **Picture.** Three cards over the empty UI (`t0258`): **Orchestrator Agent** (unified interface) · **CRUD** for agents (agents at scale) · **Observability** (performance, cost, results).
- **Worked example.** Fire one prompt → three agents appear in the left rail, each with a live status, model, cost, and context bar; the center EventStream shows every response/tool/thinking/hook; the right panel shows the orchestrator's dispatch summary. That's all three pillars in one screen ([`t0402`]).
- **Name it.** **The three pillars of multi-agent orchestration.** *"When you combine these three, you get a powerful solution… This is you controlling your compute at scale."*
- **Failure to avoid.** Treating observability as a nice dashboard, or forgetting CRUD. Drop a pillar and you either fly blind or can't manage the fleet.
- **Retrieval.** *Name the three pillars and what each unlocks.* (Orchestrator = single interface; CRUD = agents at scale; Observability = control at scale.)

---

## 4. Observability is key — *measure it or you can't scale it*

- **Hook.** Why build a whole observability UI instead of just reading terminal output? *"Observability is a key component of a successful multi-agent system."*
- **Picture.** [`t0690`] the Consumed-vs-Produced ledger with inline **Show Diff** and an **Export File Activity** button; filter tabs **RESPONSE / TOOL / THINKING / HOOK**; per-agent chips; regex search; Auto-Follow.
- **Worked example.** *"If something went wrong, I could dial in right here and understand why, when, and where, and who. What agent messed up? Was it our planner? Was it our builder?"* You can one-click into any produced file and read the diff — in the loop only as long as you need.
- **Name it.** **Observability as a pillar** — *"If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. And if you can't measure it, you can't scale it."*
- **Failure to avoid.** Ten agents doing the wrong thing feels productive and isn't. Without measurement you can't tell.
- **Retrieval.** *Complete the couplet and give the pipeline.* ("can't measure → can't improve/scale"; SDK/hook event → Postgres (`agent_logs`) → WebSocket → Pinia store → UI, + a Haiku one-sentence summary.)

---

## 5. Primary agents, not sub-agents (the differentiator)

- **Hook.** Every engineer's first objection: *"Aren't these just sub-agents? Why aren't you just using sub-agents?"*
- **Picture.** An agent card that stays put with a template badge, a running cost, and a re-promptable session — versus a Task sub-agent that fires once and vanishes.
- **Worked example.** *"Instead of just using a sub-agent here, we can turn this into a full-on primary agent by blowing away the system prompt and by giving it custom tools… You can't do all this with a sub-agent. You're locked in, it's too narrow."* In code: `create_agent(subagent_template="scout-report-suggest-fast")` resolves the `.claude/agents/*.md` template into a **fresh `ClaudeSDKClient`** (its own session), and `command_agent` re-mounts it with `resume=session_id` so it remembers.
- **Name it.** **Primary agents** (re-promptable, persistent, produce results, can themselves run slash commands/skills/sub-agents) vs **sub-agents** (ephemeral, narrow, context blown away). Building one = **pull a sub-agent template up a level** (overwrite prompt + custom tools).
- **Failure to avoid.** Dismissing the whole system as "just sub-agents" and missing what persistence + re-prompting + concrete results buys you.
- **Retrieval.** *Give two concrete things a primary agent can do that a Task sub-agent can't.* (Be re-commanded with memory via `resume=`; run its own slash commands/skills/sub-agents; produce an inspectable artifact you keep.)

---

## 6. Manage the core four of every agent — and protect the orchestrator's context (R&D)

- **Hook.** All the UI, all the features — what are you actually looking at? *"It's all just the core four."*
- **Picture.** [`t0528`] the **CONTEXT / MODEL / PROMPT / TOOLS** Venn over the live per-agent cards (context bar `x/200k`, model badge, cost).
- **Worked example.** *"We're managing the core four of every single agent we spin up. If you do not adopt your agent's perspective… you do not know what you can do."* The orchestrator keeps *its own* context minimal by **Reducing** and **Delegating** (the R&D framework from AH-1): *"it is not always observing the logs. It cannot be. We have to protect its context window."* Even after conducting huge work, the orchestrator card shows ~4–41k/200k because context is reduced + delegated.
- **Name it.** **Core four at scale** + **R&D (Reduce & Delegate)**. The system prompt even sets `COMMAND_LEVEL_COMPACT_PERCENTAGE: 80%` — at ~80% it suggests `command_agent(agent, '/compact')`.
- **Failure to avoid.** Making the orchestrator read every agent log to "stay informed" — that blows up the one context window you most need thin.
- **Retrieval.** *Why does the orchestrator's context window stay small? Which two R&D verbs?* (It never does the work or reads all logs — it Reduces its own context and Delegates to focused agents.)

---

## 7. Stay out the loop — the PITER system (tactic 4)

- **Hook.** *"This is quite literally a prompt input…"* Why a database and WebSockets instead of a chat window?
- **Picture.** A 4-stage out-loop pipeline: **P**rompt input → **T**rigger (HTTP) → **E**nvironment → **R**eview (observability). (Render as a diagram; see frame-plan `unframed_beats`.)
- **Worked example.** Prompt = your Cmd+K message (`POST /send_chat`). Trigger = the HTTP request to the FastAPI server (fired as a background task). Environment = the working directory the agents operate in (here, the app's own codebase — *"we are using the system to build the system"*). Review = observability. *"We are observing work from our agents outside the loop… Remember tactic four, stay out the loop."*
- **Name it.** **PITER** (out-loop system). ⚠️ The auto-transcript renders it **"Peter"**; the loot-box notes spell it out; it is **not** a string in the repo — it's a lesson concept mapped onto real mechanics.
- **Failure to avoid.** Reading "out of the loop" as "unsupervised and hoping." The **R** is Review — you still inspect results; you just don't type back-and-forth prompts.
- **Retrieval.** *Expand PITER and name the tactic.* (Prompt input → Trigger (HTTP) → Environment → Review; tactic 4, stay out the loop.)

---

## 8. One agent, one prompt, one purpose — then delete (tactic 6)

- **Hook.** *"There's a journey every engineer goes through… you learn that the best code is no code at all. You learn to delete."*
- **Picture.** [`t1143`] three `delete_agent{agent_name}` calls, then **"✅ All agents deleted successfully!"** — the fleet cleared, ready for the next task.
- **Worked example.** Focus each agent on a single task with a protected window, let it produce its result, then delete it. *"You must treat your agents as deletable temporary resources that serve a single purpose."* A 200K window is plenty — *"you're just stuffing a single agent with too much work, just like your boss did to you at your last job."* Sidesteps context rot / pollution / toxic context.
- **Name it.** **One agent, one prompt, one purpose** (TAC lesson 6, *Let Your Agents Focus*).
- **Failure to avoid.** Hoarding stale, context-polluted agents. The *produced artifacts* persist; the agent is disposable — *"let the agents go home… delete it, back to the data center."*
- **Retrieval.** *State the three-word rule and the 200K claim.* (One agent, one prompt, one purpose; 200K is plenty — overloading one agent, not window size, is the problem.)

---

## 9. Every agent produces a concrete result — and you template YOUR engineering into it

- **Hook.** *"Every agent should produce some concrete result. Otherwise, what was the point in the first place?"*
- **Picture.** [`t2148`] a **✅ Scout Report Complete** with a produced `app_docs/header-pills-scout-report.md (+363)` and its consumed files — a durable artifact you can review after the agent is gone.
- **Worked example.** The scout agent reports in *your* dedicated structure because you **templated your engineering** into its system prompt. *"We've templated our engineering… a dedicated scout report, a dedicated structure."* That embedded specialization is your **defensibility**: *"If it's just one, two, three, four prompts away with zero effort… how defensible is your work really?"* Out-of-the-box tools are built for everyone's codebase, not yours.
- **Name it.** **Results-oriented engineering** + **templating your engineering** (the moat).
- **Failure to avoid.** Shipping the orchestrator app with none of *your* specialized prompts/tools/agents inside it — an undifferentiated tool with no edge.
- **Retrieval.** *Why must every agent produce an artifact, and where does defensibility come from?* (So work is inspectable/handed-off and outlives the agent; defensibility comes from the specialized engineering you template in, not the app shell.)

---

## 10. The orchestrator is glue — ecosystem interop + orchestration prompts (ADWs)

- **Hook.** *"It is interoperable with the entire Claude Code ecosystem."*
- **Picture.** [`t1445`] the orchestrator spins up a `codebase-questioner` (Haiku) and commands it to run **`/question`** → *"Yes, both your orchestrator and agents can use Skills."* A **`/prime`** is mid-type. Slash commands, skills, agent templates, hooks — all plug in.
- **Worked example.** Because you can specialize prompts for a custom agent, you get **orchestration prompts**: `/orch_plan_w_scouts_build_review` is a **plan → build → review → report** three-phase **ADW**. [`t2625`] all three agents up front — a *dynamic* planner (custom prompt, no template), a `build-agent` builder, a `review-agent` reviewer; the planner consumes real Vue files and produces `specs/responsive-ui-plan.md`. The orchestrator is the **glue**: *"I think this is vastly superior to agent hand-offs… more superior to blind sub-agents."* Its **sleep-check** monitoring — [`t3215`] `Bash{command:"sleep 20"}` + `check_agent_status` — is **prompt-driven** (the workflow file sets `SLEEP_INTERVAL: 15 seconds`), *not* hidden Python.
- **Name it.** **Ecosystem interoperability** + **orchestration prompts / ADWs** + **the orchestrator as glue** (the sleep-check loop).
- **Failure to avoid.** Assuming the ~15s monitor is machinery you can't change. It lives in the workflow command — read it, edit it.
- **Retrieval.** *What are the three phases of the demo workflow, and how does the ~15s loop work?* (Plan → Build → Review (+ report); the orchestrator runs Bash(sleep 15) + check_agent_status until a `response` is followed by a `hook` `Stop`.)

---

## 11. The agentic layer, prioritize agentics (tactic 8), and operating in the gray

- **Hook.** *"Make no mistake, the multi-agent orchestration, your O-agent, it is a part of your agentic layer."*
- **Picture.** The O-agent as both a piece of the agentic layer **and** *"the key to unlocking how to best organize, create, and use your agentic layer"* — usable **before** you have a full layer.
- **Worked example.** Prioritize agentics (TAC lesson 8): *"More than 50% of your time, as a rough guideline, should be spent investing into your agentic layer, into the system that builds the system."* But be honest — this costs upfront investment and ongoing maintenance (orchestrator, Postgres, WebSockets): *"another piece of your agentic layer you'll have to maintain."* And the big missing piece is deterministic **AI Developer Workflows**: *"How does this plug into deterministic code?… We're missing our AI developer workflows. This is the big missing piece."*
- **Name it.** **Prioritize agentics** + **operating in the gray**. *"Engineering happens in the gray. It happens in the messiness of it all."*
- **Failure to avoid.** Waiting for a "finished" out-loop utopia, or selling one. Dan explicitly refuses that: it works in **and** out of the loop, and you step between modes.
- **Retrieval.** *What's the >50% guideline, and the single biggest missing piece?* (Spend >50% of your time on the agentic layer; the missing piece is deterministic-code / ADW integration — a future lesson.)

---

## The fleet at a glance

**The 8 orchestrator (management) tools — the "CRUD":**

| Tool | CRUD | Signature (verified in `agent_manager.py` + palette frame `t0300`) |
|---|---|---|
| `create_agent` | **C** | `create_agent(name, system_prompt?, model?, subagent_template?)` |
| `list_agents` | R | `list_agents()` |
| `command_agent` | C-task / **U** | `command_agent(agent_name, command)` — also `/compact` at 80% |
| `check_agent_status` | R | `check_agent_status(agent_name, tail_count=10, offset=0, verbose_logs=false)` — the sleep-check poll |
| `delete_agent` | **D** | `delete_agent(agent_name)` |
| `interrupt_agent` | D/U | `interrupt_agent(agent_name)` |
| `read_system_logs` | R | `read_system_logs(offset=0, limit=50, message_contains?, level?)` |
| `report_cost` | R | `report_cost()` — orchestrator tokens/cost/context%/session id |

**The agent templates (`.claude/agents/*.md`):**

| Template | Model | Tools | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scout-report-suggest-fast` | Haiku | Read, Glob, Grep | read-only "scout fast" → SCOUT REPORT (demoed by name) |
| `scout-report-suggest` | Sonnet | Read, Glob, Grep | deeper read-only scout |
| `build-agent` | Sonnet | Write, Read, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash, TodoWrite | implement one file from a spec (the builder) |
| `review-agent` | Sonnet | Write, Read, Bash, Grep, Glob | diff-review → Blocker/High/Med/Low → PASS/FAIL |
| `meta-agent` | Opus | Write, WebFetch, firecrawl, MultiEdit | agent architect (generates sub-agents) |
| `docs-scraper` | Haiku | firecrawl, WebFetch, Write, Edit | scrape URL → `ai_docs/` markdown |
| `playwright-validator` | Sonnet | 19× `mcp__playwright__browser_*` + Write/Edit | drive browser, screenshot, validate |

*The **planner** has no static template — it's created dynamically (custom prompt, no template) by the plan→build→review workflow. Frame `t2625` shows the planner card with no template badge.*

**Models (from `config.py`):** Sonnet `claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` (orchestrator + primary/build/review) · Haiku `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` (scouts, docs-scraper, AI summaries) · Opus (meta-agent). On-screen badges: **SONNET-4.5 / HAIKU-4.5**.

## Glossary

- **O-agent / OA / Orchestrator Agent** — the single custom agent that manages the fleet; system prompt overwritten; 8 management tools.
- **Single interface pattern** — one interface in front of many; here, one agent commanding a fleet.
- **Three pillars** — Orchestrator + CRUD-for-agents + Observability.
- **CRUD for agents** — create/command(+read status)/update/delete over agents.
- **Primary agent** — a persistent, re-promptable spawned `ClaudeSDKClient` (own session), vs an ephemeral Task **sub-agent**.
- **Agent template** — a `.claude/agents/*.md` sub-agent definition resolved into a primary agent via `create_agent(subagent_template=...)`.
- **PITER** — out-loop system: Prompt input → Trigger (HTTP) → Environment → Review (observability). *(Transcribed "Peter"; not in the repo.)*
- **Sleep-check loop** — prompt-driven `Bash(sleep 15)` + `check_agent_status` monitoring in the workflow commands.
- **ADW** — AI Developer Workflow (plan → build → review → report), here as an orchestration prompt.
- **R&D framework** — Reduce (context) & Delegate (work) — from AH-1.
- **Consumed vs Produced** — files an agent Read vs Wrote/Edited (via `file_tracker.py`), shown with inline diffs.
- **The agentic layer** — the system that builds the system; the O-agent is part of it and the key to organizing it.

## Transcript-artifact key (auto-generated VTT)

- "Peter" → **PITER**; "Cloud Code" / "clog code" → **Claude Code**; "O agent" / "OA" → **Orchestrator Agent**; "ultra thinking" → **ultrathink**; "agent decoding" → **agentic coding**; "Oracle Shure agent" → **orchestrator agent**; "Agenta Horizon" → **Agentic Horizon**; "PITER/Peter framework" is the out-loop review system (tactic 4).

## Cross-references

- **AH-1 (R&D framework / context window mastery):** the Reduce-and-Delegate engine that keeps the orchestrator thin.
- **AH-2 (agentic prompt formats):** the shape of the orchestration prompts and workflow commands.
- **AH-3 (building custom agents):** the O-agent IS a custom agent — same Claude Agent SDK, same "system prompt is the law," same core-four-in-code, same in-memory MCP custom tools, now used to build a fleet-manager. Orchestration is the rung after custom.
- **TAC 4 (AFK / stay out the loop):** PITER = the out-loop system.
- **TAC 6 (let your agents focus):** one agent, one prompt, one purpose.
- **TAC 8 (the agentic layer / prioritize agentics):** the O-agent is part of and the key to the agentic layer; >50% of your time.
- **Forward:** AH-5/AH-6 and future lessons wire this to deterministic AI Developer Workflows — the acknowledged missing piece.

# AH-4 Nuggets — ranked for the struggling learner

Ordering rule: how much of *multi-agent-orchestration competence* collapses if this nugget is missing. **Tier 1** is the paradigm you must not miss; **Tier 2** is the working machinery of the O-agent (the SDK, the tools, observability); **Tier 3** is judgment — how to run a fleet well and when it's worth building.

---

## Tier 1 — If you remember nothing else

**1. The interface is the wall; orchestration is the next rung.**
Better → more → custom agents got you here, but *"you can't scale by hopping into one terminal at a time, writing one prompt at a time."* The full ladder is **Base → Better → More → Custom → Orchestrated**, and *"the rate at which you can create and command your agents becomes the constraint of your engineering output."*
*Say it Dan's way:* "When your agents are slow, you're slow. When your agents have a problem, you have a problem."

**2. Multi-agent orchestration = three pillars, not one.**
**Orchestrator Agent** (single interface) + **CRUD-for-agents** (agents at scale) + **Observability** (performance, cost, results). *"When you combine these three, you get a powerful solution… This is you controlling your compute at scale."* Drop a pillar and you fly blind or can't manage the fleet.

**3. The Orchestrator is a custom agent — and it must NOT do the work.**
*"The orchestrator agent is a custom agent… Its system prompt is completely overwritten. Its tools are specialized. It's designed to manage other agents."* Its whole job is to orchestrate; *"we don't want our orchestrator agent getting involved in the actual work."* That's why its context window stays tiny.
*Why weak learners lose it:* they think orchestration means one big smart agent doing everything. It's the opposite — a thin conductor delegating to focused agents.

**4. Observability is a pillar, not a dashboard.**
*"If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. And if you can't measure it, you can't scale it. If you have 10 agents doing the wrong thing, does it matter that you have 10? Of course not."* You must see and filter every response/tool/thinking/hook, per agent, plus consumed-vs-produced files with diffs.

**5. Command PRIMARY agents, not blind sub-agents.**
Primary agents persist (own session, `resume=`), are re-promptable until done, produce inspectable results, and can run slash commands/skills/their own sub-agents. You build one by pulling a sub-agent template **up a level** — overwrite its system prompt + give it custom tools. *"You can't do all this with a sub-agent. You're locked in, it's too narrow."*

---

## Tier 2 — The working machinery (the O-agent)

**6. The 8 management tools ARE the CRUD.**
`create_agent(name, system_prompt?, model?, subagent_template?)` (C) · `list_agents()` / `check_agent_status(agent_name, tail_count, offset, verbose_logs)` / `read_system_logs(...)` / `report_cost()` (R) · `command_agent(agent_name, command)` (create-a-task/U) · `delete_agent` + `interrupt_agent` (D). They're an **in-memory MCP server** (`create_sdk_mcp_server('mgmt')`) — the same custom-tool pattern from AH-3, now for managing agents. The mermaid diagram labels them *"Agent Manager — 8 Management Tools."*

**7. Agent templates spawn primary agents.**
`.claude/agents/*.md` files (name/description/tools/model/color + body) are resolved by `create_agent(subagent_template=...)` into a fresh `ClaudeSDKClient`. Demoed: **scout-report-suggest-fast** (Haiku, read-only Read/Glob/Grep), **build-agent** (Sonnet, can write), **review-agent** (Sonnet, diff→PASS/FAIL). The **planner** has *no* template — it's created dynamically with a custom prompt.

**8. Same Claude Agent SDK, used twice.**
Universal loop — **options (core four) → mount `ClaudeSDKClient` → `query()` → manage the response stream** — runs for the orchestrator AND every spawned agent. This repo already uses the current names (`claude-agent-sdk` / `ClaudeAgentOptions` / `ClaudeSDKClient`), and Dan *says* "Claude Agent SDK" on camera. Blocks: `TextBlock`/`ThinkingBlock`/`ToolUseBlock`; `ResultMessage` carries session id + cost.

**9. Match the model to the job — at fleet scale.**
Orchestrator + primary/build/review = **Sonnet** (`claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`); fast scouts + docs-scraper + AI summaries = **Haiku** (`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`); the meta-agent template = **Opus**. # AH-4 — Outdated vs Current

Course-era detail → 2026 reality, with the book treatment for each. **Good news first, because it flips the AH-3 story:** this lesson's repo is already on the **current Claude Agent SDK** (`claude-agent-sdk` / `ClaudeAgentOptions` / `ClaudeSDKClient`, verified in every import and `pyproject.toml`), and **Dan actually says "the Claude Agent SDK" on camera.** So the single biggest AH-3 correction — the SDK rename — **does not apply here.** What *does* need care: the lesson is a bespoke system (not a product), it names its own biggest missing piece, and there are a few internal staleness bugs in the repo.

---

## 1. The lesson names its OWN biggest gap: no deterministic AI Developer Workflows yet ⭐

**What the lesson shows/says:** A very *agentic* system — the autonomy knob turned up. Dan is explicit about what's missing: *"How does this plug into deterministic code?… We're missing our AI developer workflows. Okay. This is the big missing piece. And this is something that we will be building… in upcoming Agentic Horizon lessons."*

**What's true now:** The O-agent is the **intermediate step** — the thing you use *while* you build an agentic layer, before you have concrete ADWs/triggers wired in. Integrating it with deterministic code (ADWs) is forward-looking, not shipped.

**Book treatment:** Present the O-agent as a **paradigm and a reference implementation**, not a finished agentic layer. Set the expectation Dan sets: this is a critical step, ADW integration comes later, and *"engineering happens in the gray."* Don't let a reader think the codebase is a plug-and-play out-loop machine.

---

## 2. The repo already uses the current SDK — state it, don't "correct" it

**What the lesson shows:** On-screen code and narration both use the **Claude Agent SDK** (`claude_agent_sdk`, `ClaudeAgentOptions`, `ClaudeSDKClient`, `create_sdk_mcp_server`, `@tool`, `HookMatcher`).

**What's true now:** Identical — this is the current SDK. (Contrast AH-3, where Dan said "Claude Code SDK" over already-renamed code.)

**Book treatment:** A one-line reassurance callout: *"The SDK names in this lesson are current — `claude-agent-sdk` / `ClaudeAgentOptions`."* Then teach the durable primitive (options = the core four → mount `ClaudeSDKClient` → `query()` → manage the response stream), and mark specific message/block field names as "current at recording; re-check the SDK reference," since those still drift.

---

## 3. Course-era model IDs — and a real internal inconsistency in the repo

**What the lesson shows:** On-screen badges read **SONNET-4.5** and **HAIKU-4.5**; `config.py` pins `DEFAULT_MODEL = claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929` and `FAST_MODEL = claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`; the meta-agent template uses Opus.

**What's true now / the bug:** The orchestrator **system prompt** (`orchestrator_agent_system_prompt.md`) still documents `haiku`/`fast` → **`claude-3-5-haiku-20241022`** (old 3.5 Haiku), while the code resolves those aliases to **`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`**. The app README also shows a stale example `ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-20250514`. The **code is source of truth.**

**Book treatment:** Keep IDs as period-accurate quotes, but teach the **principle** (Haiku-class for scouts/summaries/high-volume; Sonnet-class for primary work; Opus-class for the meta-agent). Footnote the system-prompt/README staleness so a careful reader trusts the code + the on-screen 4.5 badges, and never hardcode a model ID as a takeaway.

---

## 4. Stale docs & ports inside the repo (use the code/scripts as truth)

**What the lesson/repo shows:** The inner `apps/orchestrator_3_stream/CLAUDE.md` says backend **"port 8002"** and references files that **no longer exist** (`src/data/testData.ts`, a `ThinkingBlockRow`); `types.d.ts`'s `WSMessage` union is vestigial; `src/components/ColorChangeBox/` is an empty dir.

**What's true on disk:** Backend runs on **9403** (README + `.env` + `start_be.sh` + the frontend all agree); frontend on **5175**. `modules/hooks.py` is **legacy/orphan** (no importers) — the active hooks are `command_agent_hooks.py` + `orchestrator_hooks.py`.

**Book treatment:** In the lab, tell students to trust `start_be.sh` / `.env` / the running app over the doc comments (ports **9403 / 5175**). Mention `hooks.py` is dead code so no one studies the wrong file. These are ordinary repo-drift gotchas, not lesson errors.

---

## 5. This is a private, bespoke system — the pattern is the payload, not the app

**What the lesson shows:** A polished custom Vue + FastAPI + Postgres observability app.

**What's true now:** Dan is emphatic it is **not a product you must adopt:** *"I'm not here to tell you how to set up your multi-agent orchestration or even that you need to use this… I don't care what user interface you use."* Big labs are shipping primitive one-agent-at-a-time versions; this is the paradigm ahead of them.

**Book treatment:** Frame the codebase as a **reference implementation to learn the pattern from** (single interface + CRUD-for-agents + observability + out-loop), explicitly transferable to *any* tool — even a plain terminal. Don't teach it as a dependency; teach the three pillars.

---

## 6. Config-path & setup gotchas (lab-relevant)

**What's true on disk:** The backend's `config.py` computes `PROJECT_ROOT` so it loads **`apps/orchestrator_3_stream/.env`**, *not* the repo-root `.env` — and there are two divergent `.env.sample` files. `.mcp.json.sample` must be renamed to `.mcp.json` (three servers: playwright, neon, firecrawl). DB migrations need `psql` on PATH.

**Book treatment:** Call these out in the **lab setup** (copy `.env` into the app dir; rename `.mcp.json`; ensure `psql`), the same way AH-3 flagged the Firecrawl `.sample` rename. Small, real, and otherwise silently confusing.

---

## 7. Features Dan explicitly marks as MISSING / future — don't present them as present

- **Human-in-the-loop decision points** (agents asking *you* questions) — *"That's missing here."*
- **Better orchestration-agent management + multiple codebases through one UI** — the server currently targets **one `--cwd` at a time**.
- **Forking an agent's context window** / duplicating an agent from a point — *"one tool away… a few modules away."*
- **Prompt-engineering autocomplete/tab** (a cheap fast model in the terminal) — *"the highest return on investment."*

**Book treatment:** Keep these in a clearly-labeled "future directions / not-yet-built" box so a reader doesn't go looking for them in the codebase.

---

## What has NOT aged (teach as current, verbatim)

- **The scale framework** — Base → Better → More → Custom → Orchestrated; scale compute to scale impact. Timeless.
- **The three pillars** — Orchestrator + CRUD-for-agents + Observability. Model-agnostic architecture.
- **Observability is a pillar** — "can't measure → can't improve/scale"; results-oriented, filterable, diff-able.
- **Primary agents vs sub-agents** — persistent/re-promptable vs ephemeral; pull a template up a level.
- **Core four at scale + R&D** — read any agent by its core four; keep the orchestrator thin.
- **PITER out-loop (tactic 4), one-agent-one-prompt-one-purpose (tactic 6), prioritize-agentics (tactic 8).** Durable tactics.
- **Template your engineering / defensibility** — specialization is the moat; out-of-the-box tools serve everyone's codebase, not yours.
- **The sleep-check loop as prompt-driven glue; every agent produces a concrete result.** Patterns, not tool trivia.
- **The O-agent is part of, and the key to, the agentic layer** — usable before the layer exists. The most durable claim of the lesson.

---

## Strict YouTube-overlay decision (map-to-lesson / named-gap only)

Two candidates map to *this lesson's* named holes with no topic drift; both `include_in_phase1 = true`, both `verify_before_publish = true` (IDs carried from the tac-1 seed list; no video was fetched, per brief — confirm each resolves and re-check the title before shipping the link):

| video_id | title | maps_to | why it's allowed |
|----------|-------|---------|------------------|
| `fop_yxV-mPo` | Codebase Singularity | named hole (Gap 1/5) | The O-agent is *"the key to unlocking how to best organize, create, and use your agentic layer"* and the self-operating-codebase end-state. Deferred from tac-1 as "too much scale for lesson 1" — AH-4 **is** the scale chapter, so it's now on-topic. |
| `6fCqj4xFCZI` | How Claude Code CHANGED Engineering Forever | named hole (Gap 2/5) | The whole system rests on *"the Claude Agent SDK and the ecosystem… far ahead of the pack… the extensibility of this tool."* Bridges that claim to the current state of the SDK/ecosystem. |

**Deferred (do not surface on this chapter):** `X2ciJedw2vU` (ZERO to Agent SKILL) — the lesson confirms "orchestrator and agents can use skills," so a Skills primer *maps*, but Skills are the heart of the AH-3/skills lessons, not the orchestration chapter. Keep it in the volume map (`include_in_phase1 = false`). Broader "AI-labs multi-agent product" videos would drift into speculation — Dan makes the "big labs will build this" point himself; no overlay needed.

# AH-4 Lab Spec — Multi-Agent Orchestration: The O-Agent

**Scope rule:** every drill runs inside the course codebase only — `agentic-horizon/multi-agent-orchestration` (resolve the lesson symlink `.../ah-4-multi-agent-orchestration-the-o-agent/codebase`, or clone from the loot box: `git clone https://github.com/disler/multi-agent-orchestration.git`). No external repos. The app points at its own codebase (`--cwd apps/orchestrator_3_stream`), so you are literally using the system to build the system.
**Prime directive (graded throughout):** you command the fleet **through the Orchestrator** (Cmd+K) — you never hop into a side terminal to hand-run an agent, and you never hand-edit an agent to "fix" it. You're learning to conduct, not to babysit.
**Reading skill graded above all:** for every agent you touch — the orchestrator and each spawned agent — you must be able to point at its **core four** (context, model, prompt, tools) and name how each is set.
**Time box:** 120–180 minutes (advanced; real infra: Postgres + backend + frontend). **Token/cost note:** fan-out burns real tokens — the fast scouts are Haiku (cheap), but plan→build→review with Sonnet agents adds up. Budget for it, and **delete your agents** when done (it's also the lesson).

---

## 0 · Setup (25–35 min) — real infrastructure

1. Enter the codebase and read the top-level `README.md` (the 8 tools + the architecture diagram) and root `CLAUDE.md` (engineering rules: no-mock tests, UV only, keep `models.py` in sync).
2. **Toolbelt:** `uv --version`, `claude --version`, `node --version`, `bun --version`, and **`psql --version`** (needed for migrations).
3. **Database:** create a **Neon** serverless Postgres (recommended) *or* a local/Docker Postgres. Put its DSN in `DATABASE_URL`.
4. **Env:** `cp .env.sample .env`; set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` + `DATABASE_URL`. **Copy the root `.env` into both app dirs** (`apps/orchestrator_3_stream/.env` and `apps/orchestrator_db/.env`) — the backend loads the app-dir `.env`, *not* the repo root.
5. **Migrations:** `uv run apps/orchestrator_db/run_migrations.py` → confirm 6 tables (`orchestrator_agents`, `agents`, `prompts`, `agent_logs`, `system_logs`, `orchestrator_chat`).
6. **Backend:** `cd apps/orchestrator_3_stream && ./start_be.sh` → serves **http://127.0.0.1:9403** (ignore the inner `CLAUDE.md`'s stale "8002").
7. **Frontend:** `bun install` then `./start_fe.sh` → open **http://127.0.0.1:5175**. You should see the empty shell: `AGENTS 0 Total`, `Active/Running/Logs 0`, `Cost $0.00`, and *"Start a conversation."*
8. **SDK sanity:** open `backend/pyproject.toml` + any backend module — confirm `claude-agent-sdk` / `from claude_agent_sdk import … ClaudeAgentOptions, ClaudeSDKClient`. (Unlike AH-3, the names here are already current — Dan even says "Claude Agent SDK.")

**Checkpoint 0:** the app is live at :5175, connected (green dot), 6 tables exist, and you can state the backend port (**9403**) and the SDK name (**claude-agent-sdk**) without looking.

---

## 1 · Reading drill — the O-agent's core four + the 8 tools (20 min)

Open `backend/prompts/orchestrator_agent_system_prompt.md` and `backend/modules/agent_manager.py`. Write down:
- The **first line** of the system prompt (what IS the orchestrator?).
- The **8 management tools** and, for each, its params — then label each **C/R/U/D**.
- How the orchestrator's **core four** is set in `orchestrator_service.py`: model (`ORCHESTRATOR_MODEL`), system_prompt (overwritten), tools (`create_sdk_mcp_server('mgmt')` + `Bash, Read, SlashCommand, Skill`), context (200k window, R&D).

**Checkpoint 1:** your list has all 8 tools with correct CRUD labels (create_agent=C; list_agents/check_agent_status/read_system_logs/report_cost=R; command_agent=U/task; delete_agent+interrupt_agent=D), and you can say why the orchestrator's system prompt is a **full overwrite** (it's a custom meta-agent, not Claude Code).

---

## 2 · Run the fleet & feel the "3× compute" (20 min)

1. Cmd+K → ping the orchestrator (`ping`). Confirm a quick response and that **no agents** were created (it answered directly).
2. Cmd+K → *"Create three agents to summarize this codebase: one for the frontend, one for the backend, and a primary QA agent to summarize both into a full-stack architecture doc with a Mermaid diagram."*
3. Watch the EventStream: count the orchestrator's tool calls (**expect 6** — 3× `create_agent` + 3× `command_agent`). In the left rail, read each agent's **model badge** (2× Haiku fast + 1× Sonnet primary), cost, and context bar.

**Checkpoint 2:** you can point at the 6 tool calls and say, in one sentence, why this is *"three times the compute an engineer in a terminal has"* — and identify which agents are fast (Haiku) vs primary (Sonnet).

---

## 3 · Observability drill — the pillar in action (20 min) ⭐

This is the money drill.
1. Use the filter tabs: **RESPONSE / TOOL / THINKING / HOOK**. Then filter to a **single agent** via its chip. Then run a **regex** search over events.
2. When the QA agent finishes, open its **Consumed vs Produced** panel: click **Show Diff** on a produced `.md`, then **one-click into your editor** (that's `POST /api/open-file`). Read the produced architecture doc — trace the mermaid: browser → FastAPI → Orchestrator Service → Orchestrator Agent (Sonnet 4.5) → Management Tools MCP Server / Agent Manager (8 tools).
3. Read each agent card's **core four** (context bar `x/200k`, model, cost, tool/hook/response/thinking counts).

**Checkpoint 3 (write it down):** *observability is why you can (a) see every agent's core four at a glance, (b) diff and open produced files, and (c) debug "which agent did what."* State the couplet: **"if you can't measure it, you can't improve it — and you can't scale it."**

---

## 4 · CRUD drill — create, command, check, delete (15 min)

1. Ask the orchestrator to **list agents and check their status** — watch it run `list_agents` / `check_agent_status`. Note it does **not** dump every log (it protects its own context).
2. Re-command one existing agent with a follow-up (proves **update / re-prompt** with memory).
3. Cmd+K → **"delete all agents."** Watch N× `delete_agent` + *"✅ All agents deleted successfully."* Confirm `AGENTS 0 Total` and that the **produced docs still exist** in `app_docs/`.

**Checkpoint 4:** you can explain "treat your agents as deletable temporary resources that serve a single purpose" — the work (artifacts) persisted, the agents did not. You can also explain why the orchestrator *shouldn't* keep reading all logs (protect its context / R&D).

---

## 5 · Ecosystem + templates — primary vs sub-agent (25 min)

1. **Slash-command interop:** Cmd+K → *"Create an agent and command it to run `/question`: can the orchestrator and its agents use skills?"* Read the produced answer (**yes**). Then have an agent run **`/prime`** and note the context it loads.
2. **Template creation:** Cmd+K → *"Create an agent with the `scout-report-suggest-fast` template and command it to summarize which fields our regex search looks at."* Open `.claude/agents/scout-report-suggest-fast.md` and confirm its frontmatter (**model haiku; tools Read, Glob, Grep**). Note that `create_agent(subagent_template=…)` turned that sub-agent template into a **primary** agent (its own card, re-promptable).

**Checkpoint 5:** you can state, in your own words, why this is a **primary agent, not a sub-agent** ("pulled up a level" — own session, re-promptable, runs slash commands/skills), and confirm from `meta-prompt/SKILL.md` that commands are kept model-invocable ("DO NOT use `disable-model-invocation`") so agents can trigger them.

---

## 6 · The ADW workflow + the sleep-check glue (25 min)

Pick **one** orchestration workflow and run it end-to-end via Cmd+K.

**A. Scout + Build** (`/orch_scout_and_build`): a small UI tweak (e.g. "add simple flat gray info pills to the app header"). Watch the orchestrator create a **scout** (`scout-report-suggest-fast`) + a **builder** (`build-agent`), then **sleep + `check_agent_status`** while they work.

**B. Plan → Build → Review** (`/orch_plan_w_scouts_build_review`): a responsive-UI change (e.g. "collapse the agent list and shrink the orchestrator chat under 650px"). Watch all three agents get created up front — a **dynamic planner** (custom prompt, *no* template), a **`build-agent`** builder, a **`review-agent`** reviewer — and the three phases run with a **final report**; the reviewer verifies the vite build.

Then open the workflow command file (`apps/orchestrator_3_stream/.claude/commands/orch_plan_w_scouts_build_review.md`) and find `SLEEP_INTERVAL: 15 seconds` + the `Bash(sleep …)` + `check_agent_status` loop.

**Checkpoint 6:** you can (a) name the three phases and each agent's template (planner=none/dynamic, builder=`build-agent`, reviewer=`review-agent`), (b) show that the ~15s monitor is **prompt-driven** (not hidden Python), and (c) point at the completion signal (a `response` event_category followed by a `hook` `Stop`).

---

## 7 · Judgment drill — orchestrate, or not? (10 min)

Write two short lists from your own work:
1. Three jobs that are **orchestration-shaped** (multiple specialized agents, repeatable multi-phase workflow, worth out-loop review with observability).
2. Three jobs that should stay a **single agent / in-loop** (exploratory, one-off, generic, tight back-and-forth).
Then map ONE orchestration-shaped job onto **PITER**: what's the Prompt input, the Trigger, the Environment, and how would you Review it?

**Checkpoint 7:** your first orchestration pick genuinely needs a *fleet* (not one focused agent) — and you can articulate the out-loop review, not just "more agents."

---

## Stretch (optional, +30–60 min) — change the fleet *through* the system

Type zero application code by hand; make changes through the orchestrator/agents or through config.
1. **New template:** add a new `.claude/agents/<name>.md` template (frontmatter + body) and have the orchestrator `create_agent(subagent_template="<name>")`; prove it runs.
2. **New tool:** have Claude Code add a 9th management tool to `agent_manager.py` (e.g. `archive_agent`), register it in `create_sdk_mcp_server`, add it to `allowed_tools`, and prove the orchestrator can call it.
3. **New orchestration prompt:** write a new `.claude/commands/orch_*.md` workflow (use the `meta-prompt` skill) and run it.
4. **Fix a staleness bug:** update the orchestrator system prompt's stale `claude-3-5-haiku-20241022` doc line to match the code (`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`), and/or the inner `CLAUDE.md` port (8002 → 9403). Verify the app still runs.

**Stretch checkpoint:** every change went through the agent/config surface, and you can point at the `ClaudeAgentOptions` (orchestrator or spawned agent) affected by your change.

---

## Pass criteria (all must hold)

- [ ] The app is live (backend :9403, frontend :5175), connected, with 6 Postgres tables.
- [ ] You can point at the orchestrator's `ClaudeAgentOptions` and name how each of the **core four** is set (incl. its 8-tool `mgmt` MCP server).
- [ ] You created ≥3 agents from ONE prompt and can explain the "3× compute" moment.
- [ ] You used the observability UI (filters + Consumed/Produced + Show Diff + one-click-open) and stated the "can't measure → can't scale" couplet (Checkpoint 3).
- [ ] You demonstrated all four CRUD verbs and deleted the fleet (Checkpoint 4), and can explain "deletable temporary resources."
- [ ] You created an agent from the `scout-report-suggest-fast` template and can explain **primary vs sub-agent** (Checkpoint 5).
- [ ] You ran an orchestration workflow (scout+build **or** plan→build→review) and showed the **sleep-check is prompt-driven** (Checkpoint 6).
- [ ] You produced your orchestrate-vs-single-agent lists and mapped one job onto **PITER** (Checkpoint 7).

---

## Instructor / self-grader notes

- **Highest-value single drill is #3 (observability).** If a student "gets" only one thing, it must be that observability is a *pillar* — measurement is what makes a fleet controllable and scalable, not a nicety.
- **Watch for the "just sub-agents" trap.** A student who can't articulate why a *primary* agent (persistent, re-promptable, runs its own commands/skills, keeps artifacts) beats a Task sub-agent hasn't got the differentiator (Checkpoint 5).
- **Grade the orchestrator's context.** A strong student notices the orchestrator's context bar stays tiny (~4–41k/200k) even after big runs, and can explain R&D (Reduce + Delegate) as the reason.
- **The sleep-check is a common misconception.** Many assume a hidden Python poll loop. Make them open the workflow command and find `Bash(sleep 15)` + `check_agent_status` (Checkpoint 6). It's prompt-driven glue.
- **Setup will bite.** If Postgres/`psql` or the app-dir `.env` copy is missed, nothing runs — don't fail a student for the infra gotchas; treat them as the intended "operating in the gray" lesson. Trust code/scripts over the stale doc comments (ports 9403/5175; ignore `hooks.py`).
- **Cost hygiene is part of the grade.** A student who leaves a fleet running (especially Sonnet plan→build→review) burns tokens; deleting agents when done is both cost control and the lesson ("let the agents go home").
- **Don't let a student treat this app as a required product.** The transferable payload is the pattern (single interface + CRUD + observability + out-loop) — they could rebuild a thinner version in any tool.

**Checkpoint 6:** you can (a) name the three phases and each agent's template (planner=none/dynamic, builder=`build-agent`, reviewer=`review-agent`), (b) show that the ~15s monitor is **prompt-driven** (not hidden Python), and (c) point at the completion signal (a `response` event_category followed by a `hook` `Stop`).

---

## 7 · Judgment drill — orchestrate, or not? (10 min)

Write two short lists from your own work:
1. Three jobs that are **orchestration-shaped** (multiple specialized agents, repeatable multi-phase workflow, worth out-loop review with observability).
2. Three jobs that should stay a **single agent / in-loop** (exploratory, one-off, generic, tight back-and-forth).
Then map ONE orchestration-shaped job onto **PITER**: what's the Prompt input, the Trigger, the Environment, and how would you Review it?

**Checkpoint 7:** your first orchestration pick genuinely needs a *fleet* (not one focused agent) — and you can articulate the out-loop review, not just "more agents."

---

## Stretch (optional, +30–60 min) — change the fleet *through* the system

Type zero application code by hand; make changes through the orchestrator/agents or through config.
1. **New template:** add a new `.claude/agents/<name>.md` template (frontmatter + body) and have the orchestrator `create_agent(subagent_template="<name>")`; prove it runs.
2. **New tool:** have Claude Code add a 9th management tool to `agent_manager.py` (e.g. `archive_agent`), register it in `create_sdk_mcp_server`, add it to `allowed_tools`, and prove the orchestrator can call it.
3. **New orchestration prompt:** write a new `.claude/commands/orch_*.md` workflow (use the `meta-prompt` skill) and run it.
4. **Fix a staleness bug:** update the orchestrator system prompt's stale `claude-3-5-haiku-20241022` doc line to match the code (`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`), and/or the inner `CLAUDE.md` port (8002 → 9403). Verify the app still runs.

**Stretch checkpoint:** every change went through the agent/config surface, and you can point at the `ClaudeAgentOptions` (orchestrator or spawned agent) affected by your change.

---

## Pass criteria (all must hold)

- [ ] The app is live (backend :9403, frontend :5175), connected, with 6 Postgres tables.
- [ ] You can point at the orchestrator's `ClaudeAgentOptions` and name how each of the **core four** is set (incl. its 8-tool `mgmt` MCP server).
- [ ] You created ≥3 agents from ONE prompt and can explain the "3× compute" moment.
- [ ] You used the observability UI (filters + Consumed/Produced + Show Diff + one-click-open) and stated the "can't measure → can't scale" couplet (Checkpoint 3).
- [ ] You demonstrated all four CRUD verbs and deleted the fleet (Checkpoint 4), and can explain "deletable temporary resources."
- [ ] You created an agent from the `scout-report-suggest-fast` template and can explain **primary vs sub-agent** (Checkpoint 5).
- [ ] You ran an orchestration workflow (scout+build **or** plan→build→review) and showed the **sleep-check is prompt-driven** (Checkpoint 6).
- [ ] You produced your orchestrate-vs-single-agent lists and mapped one job onto **PITER** (Checkpoint 7).

---

## Instructor / self-grader notes

- **Highest-value single drill is #3 (observability).** If a student "gets" only one thing, it must be that observability is a *pillar* — measurement is what makes a fleet controllable and scalable, not a nicety.
- **Watch for the "just sub-agents" trap.** A student who can't articulate why a *primary* agent (persistent, re-promptable, runs its own commands/skills, keeps artifacts) beats a Task sub-agent hasn't got the differentiator (Checkpoint 5).
- **Grade the orchestrator's context.** A strong student notices the orchestrator's context bar stays tiny (~4–41k/200k) even after big runs, and can explain R&D (Reduce + Delegate) as the reason.
- **The sleep-check is a common misconception.** Many assume a hidden Python poll loop. Make them open the workflow command and find `Bash(sleep 15)` + `check_agent_status` (Checkpoint 6). It's prompt-driven glue.
- **Setup will bite.** If Postgres/`psql` or the app-dir `.env` copy is missed, nothing runs — don't fail a student for the infra gotchas; treat them as the intended "operating in the gray" lesson. Trust code/scripts over the stale doc comments (ports 9403/5175; ignore `hooks.py`).
- **Cost hygiene is part of the grade.** A student who leaves a fleet running (especially Sonnet plan→build→review) burns tokens; deleting agents when done is both cost control and the lesson ("let the agents go home").
- **Don't let a student treat this app as a required product.** The transferable payload is the pattern (single interface + CRUD + observability + out-loop) — they could rebuild a thinner version in any tool.
